title: TPS Dealt New Legal Blows: Full List of Communities Facing Deportation - Newsweek
description:
We are continuing the legal fight, but TPS holders need immediate and permanent protections.
Which Other TPS Countries Have Lost Status?
The rulings come as the Trump administration continues its broader effort to unwind TPS protections for multiple countries.
Judges in both the Burma and South Sudan cases noted that the Supreme Court held that the TPS statute largely bars judicial review of nonconstitutional challenges to TPS termination decisions.
The latest decisions, therefore, add Burma and South Sudan to the growing list of TPS designations whose terminations have survived major legal challenges, alongside Haiti and Syria.
text:
Two federal judges officially ended Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for two countries Friday, in the wake of the U.S. Supreme Court's decision favoring the Trump administration in June, opening up thousands more immigrants to potential deportation.

The rulings on South Sudan and Burma's statuses continue a trend of lower court judges undoing the blocks they had placed on the Department of Homeland Security's (DHS) efforts to end TPS for hundreds of thousands of immigrants—many of whom have been in the U.S. for over a decade.

Because of the Supreme Court's ruling on TPS for Haiti and Syria, in which the justices said DHS did have the authority to end protections, other similar cases covering different nationalities were also expected to fall in line.

Read More on Politics

"The Trump administration has relentlessly pursued every avenue to strip TPS holders of their lawful status with the end goal of subjecting long-term members of our communities to detention and deportation," Lupe Aguirre, deputy director of U.S. litigation at the International Refugee Assistance Project, told Newsweek on Friday.

"The Supreme Court ruling on TPS has resulted in thousands of people losing their protections with each decision from lower courts severely constrained from intervening in the Trump administration's cruel de-documentation campaign. We are continuing the legal fight, but TPS holders need immediate and permanent protections. Congress must act now to protect them."

DHS General Counsel James Percival has been celebrating the court decisions on X, taking aim at the judges who have yet to rule on the cases, posting Friday, "Every day these 'administrative stays' are in effect is a day the American people are denied what they voted for.

"Under the previous administration Temporary Protected Status was abused to allow violent terrorists, criminals, and national security threats into our nation," a DHS spokesperson told Newsweek Firday. "TPS was never designed to be permanent. With the renewed peace in South Sudan, their demonstrated commitment to ensuring the safe reintegration of returning nationals, and improved diplomatic relations, now is the right time to conclude what was always intended to be a temporary designation.”

What the Judges Said About Burma, South Sudan TPS

Federal judges in Illinois and Massachusetts largely rejected new efforts to block the Trump administration's termination of TPS for Burma and South Sudan, finding that plaintiffs were unlikely to succeed on newly advanced legal theories.

In the South Sudan case, Patti B. Saris of the U.S. District Court for Massachusetts denied a request to amend the lawsuit and renew a bid to postpone the TPS termination.

The plaintiffs argued that former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem lacked authority to end TPS and that the government violated due process protections. Saris rejected both claims, concluding that the Homeland Security secretary has long been understood to hold TPS authority and that the plaintiffs' due process arguments were unlikely to succeed.

Krish O’Mara Vignarajah, President and CEO of Global Refuge, told Newsweek Friday, “To be clear about this ruling, the court did not find that South Sudan is safe to return to. It found that after the Supreme Court's decision, federal judges have been stripped of the power to even ask if the country is safe.”

O’Mara Vignarajah said that the reality was that South Sudan was on the brink of a return to "all-out-civil war."

“With only several hundred South Sudanese holding TPS in the U.S. right now, this isn't a policy forced by scale or strain on our system," she said. "To the contrary, this is the administration’s deliberate choice to send a small group of vulnerable individuals and families back into a country where civilians are bearing the brunt of intensifying violence and displacement.”

In the Burma case, Matthew F. Kennelly of the Northern District of Illinois reached a similar conclusion on the plaintiffs' new claims, dismissing them and denying a renewed request to delay the TPS termination. Kennelly likewise found that Congress transferred TPS authority to DHS through the Homeland Security Act and said the due process claims amounted to an attempt to repackage arguments that are no longer viable after the Supreme Court's recent TPS decision.

The Illinois ruling, however, left one avenue of challenge alive. Kennelly declined to dismiss a claim alleging racial discrimination in the administration's handling of TPS terminations, finding the plaintiffs had plausibly alleged an equal protection violation at this stage. The judge left that question open for higher courts to weigh in before the case proceeds further.

How quickly U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents move to detain those who have lost status remains to be seen, after current and former officials at the agency told Newsweek Thursday that agents had been told to avoid arresting immigrants covered by the class action lawsuits for now.

Which Other TPS Countries Have Lost Status?

The rulings come as the Trump administration continues its broader effort to unwind TPS protections for multiple countries. The Supreme Court's June decision in Mullin v. Doe involved the administration's termination of TPS for Haiti and Syria and has become the key precedent shaping lower court decisions around the country.

Judges in both the Burma and South Sudan cases noted that the Supreme Court held that the TPS statute largely bars judicial review of nonconstitutional challenges to TPS termination decisions. That ruling has significantly narrowed the legal options available to advocates seeking to block the end of protections for affected groups.

The latest decisions, therefore, add Burma and South Sudan to the growing list of TPS designations whose terminations have survived major legal challenges, alongside Haiti and Syria.

The other countries that have seen TPS terminated are: Yemen, Nicaragua, Afghanistan, Nepal, Cameroon, Honduras and Venezuela.

Somalia and Ethiopia still have pending lower court cases.

Critics of the move to end TPS have said that in many of the countries affected, conditions have not improved as the government has claimed. This, they say, means immigrants face dangerous or difficult conditions should they return to their home countries.

What Happens Next?

While the protections under TPS appear to be over, and DHS is urging those covered to leave the U.S., legal representatives are still exploring other options, and some immigrants may be eligible for other legal statuses.

A federal prosecutor fired last year over critical comments he had written as a private citizen about Donald Trump sued the justice department on Friday, saying his termination violated his first amendment rights.
The September 2025 termination was part of a sweeping personnel purge over the last year and a half inside the justice department, which has fired prosecutors who worked on investigations into Trump and others seen as being against the administration’s efforts.
“Yet the Department of Justice fired him on the eve of trial because, years ago as a private citizen, he published criticisms of President Trump.
Since the current Department of Justice will not stand up for the first amendment and the American people, we will.
It has no place here.” A justice department spokeswoman declined to comment, citing pending litigation.
text:
A federal prosecutor fired last year over critical comments he had written as a private citizen about Donald Trump sued the justice department on Friday, saying his termination violated his first amendment rights.

Will Rosenzweig was two weeks away from trying a multimillion-dollar Medicare fraud case when a blog he had written years earlier covering a broad range of topics was publicized online by a conservative political commentator who also included a screenshot of Rosenzweig’s LinkedIn account and tagged senior justice department officials for their awareness.

Less than three hours after the post, the lawsuit says, Rosenzweig received an email signed by then attorney general Pam Bondi informing him that he had been fired. The news came as Rosenzweig was out of town with his family observing the Jewish holiday of Rosh Hashana.

The September 2025 termination was part of a sweeping personnel purge over the last year and a half inside the justice department, which has fired prosecutors who worked on investigations into Trump and others seen as being against the administration’s efforts.

A lawsuit filed in federal court in Miami, where Rosenzweig worked as a federal prosecutor for five years, seeks reinstatement to the job as well as backpay and a court order declaring his firing unlawful.

The complaint says Rosenzweig was a highly respected prosecutor who received “consistent praise and awards” and was so highly valued in his office that he was told just weeks before his firing that he would be getting a special parking spot due to his performance.

“Will Rosenzweig was an excellent prosecutor who returned millions of dollars to the taxpayers by prosecuting healthcare fraud cases,” said a statement from his lawyers, Margaret Donovan, Daniel Fridman and Adam Fels.

“Yet the Department of Justice fired him on the eve of trial because, years ago as a private citizen, he published criticisms of President Trump. Since the current Department of Justice will not stand up for the first amendment and the American people, we will. We look forward to vindicating Will’s rights in court.”

The blog Rosenzweig had maintained had been defunct for over six years at the time of his firing and included his thoughts on travel, sports and other “apolitical, anodyne topics” in addition to critical observations about Trump and other political candidates, the lawsuit says.

The conservative commentator, Natalie Winters, who has a large online following, characterized Rosenzweig as “a rogue Trump hater” as she posted screenshots of some of his political musings, according to the complaint, which characterizes the firing as a direct assault on Rosenzweig’s free-speech rights.

“The department’s conduct rests on a single premise: a citizen must forever refrain from criticizing the government and its leaders to remain eligible to serve it,” the lawsuit says.

“That rule would force every American who might one day serve to choose between speaking freely now and working for the government later. Conditioning public employment on political loyalty, where a party card rather than merit opens the door to a government job, is a way of life in Havana and Caracas. It has no place here.”

A justice department spokeswoman declined to comment, citing pending litigation.

text:
Human Rights Commission Hears Testimony on Anti-Immigrant Violence

The brother of an Ecuadorian immigrant who was stabbed to death on Long Island in 2008 testified Thursday before a Human Rights Commission hearing in Washington, DC.

Seven teenagers were convicted in connection with Marcelo Lucero’s death as a hate crime. They became known as the Patchogue 7.

Joselo Lucero told members of the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights: “To find out my brother was killed because he looks like me. Let’s face it, just being here in his country as a brown person, everybody that looks like me, we are {considered} criminals. I’m a citizen of this country, but I don’t feel safe, in 2008 and now in 2026.”

ICE Separated Nursing Mom From Infant, Toddler in Nashville, Against Its Own Rules, Advocates Say

A group of human rights organizations are seeking the immediate release of a breastfeeding mother with a pending asylum claim, who was detained in May by immigration agents at her home in Nashville as she was putting her two young children into a car to get to a doctor’s appointment.

In a complaint filed Wednesday with the Department of Homeland Security’s Office of Inspector General, the organizations allege that Immigration and Customs Enforcement is violating its own policies against detaining pregnant, postpartum and nursing parents and requiring ICE to facilitate visits between children and parents.

On Venezuela’s Coast, Life Is Reduced to Survival and Burial

There was a billboard on the seaside road along Venezuela’s northern coast with a gigantic photo of a smiling Nicolás Maduro, the country’s former leader, and the words “a land flowing with milk and honey,” a biblical phrase that describes a blessed land.

But there was no Mr. Maduro, no milk and no honey behind the sign. Just mountains of rubble, body bags and makeshift encampments for thousands of Venezuelans left homeless by June’s devastating, back-to-back earthquakes.

More Than a Decade After 43 Students Vanished in Mexico, Ex-Governor Arrested, Accused of Cover-Up

Mexican authorities have arrested the former governor of the southern state Guerrero for his alleged involvement in the disappearance of 43 students in 2014, a case that has become a symbol for impunity and state involvement in cartel violence.

Federal prosecutors said Thursday that they arrested Ángel Aguirre, Guerrero’s former governor, on accusations of “concealing evidence to determine the whereabouts of the students” of the Ayotzinapa Rural Teachers’ College.

In early August 2026, a rumor spread online that the White House posted Spider-Man-inspired graphics on Instagram that promoted immigration deportations.

text:
SAN DIEGO – Former U.S. Customs and Border Protection Officer Jesse Clark Garcia was sentenced in federal court today to nine years in prison for allowing drug-laden vehicles to pass through his inspection lane at the Tecate Port of Entry on behalf of the Sinaloa Cartel.

The sentencing follows a long‑term, multi‑agency investigation that uncovered a significant corruption scheme involving Garcia and his co-defendant, then-Customs and Border Protection (CBP) Officer Diego Bonillo. Both officers pleaded guilty in July 2025, with Garcia admitting that since at least 2021, he provided the Sinaloa Cartel-linked drug trafficking organization with his duty schedules and lane assignments so vehicles carrying cocaine, methamphetamine, and fentanyl could pass through his lanes unchecked. Bonillo was sentenced to 15 years in prison in November 2025.

“Officer Garcia betrayed his oath, his fellow officers, and his country. Officer Garcia’s conduct warranted this significant sentence,” said U.S. Attorney Adam Gordon.

To coordinate with the traffickers, both defendants used a secret emoji-based code in text messages to discreetly communicate their shift and lane assignments. The cartel then routed drug-laden vehicles through those lanes, where the defendants allowed them to enter the United States without inspection.

Garcia also exploited CBP’s flexible duty-switching policies to place himself in inspection lanes where he was not scheduled to work. Other times, he falsely claimed technical issues prevented required checks, allowing narcotics to enter the United States despite mandatory system alerts.

In exchange for his assistance, the Garcia received at least $10,000 for each drug-filled vehicle he allowed to pass through the port. Evidence further showed that his illicit proceeds funded a lifestyle far beyond his government salary, including luxury purchases, a high-end vehicle, a San Diego residence, co-ownership of an equine racing business, and construction of a ranch in Mexico.

As the investigation progressed, the Garcia attempted to evade law enforcement. He stopped reporting for duty, ignored inquiries from CBP supervisors, and was observed driving into Mexico in a fully packed vehicle in late March 2024. On May 2, 2024, Mexican authorities—acting on a request from the United States and pursuant to a federal warrant—arrested the defendant and transferred him to U.S. custody later that same evening.

On July 8, 2025, Garcia pleaded guilty to nine felony counts, including conspiracy to import controlled substances and multiple counts of importation and aiding and abetting. As part of his plea agreement, he admitted facilitating the entry of substantial quantities of controlled substances, including at least 100 kilograms of fentanyl, 107 kilograms of methamphetamine, and 270 kilograms of cocaine.

DHS Inspector General Joseph V. Cuffari, Ph.D., said, “DHS employees who abuse their positions and betray the public’s trust will be held accountable for their actions. The Office of Inspector General will continue to relentlessly root out corruption. We appreciate the continued partnership between DHS OIG and our law enforcement partners in bringing these individuals to justice.”

“Jesse Clark Garcia showed total disregard for the oath he took as a CBP Officer to protect our communities when he knowingly and repeatedly allowed cocaine, methamphetamine, and fentanyl into our country,” said Special Agent in Charge Mark Remily of the FBI San Diego Field Office. “FBI San Diego and our partners work tirelessly to ensure those individuals dishonoring the badge are held accountable. The corrupt few do not represent the whole of the federal law enforcement workforce. Today’s sentence demonstrates the FBI’s commitment to rooting out those unworthy individuals and paving the way for justice to be served.”

According to Special Agent in Charge Sara Esparagoza, U.S. Customs and Border Protection, Office of Professional Responsibility, San Diego Field Office, “The Office of Professional Responsibility is unwavering in its commitment to upholding the highest standards within our ranks. Today’s events underscore our dedication to rooting out corruption and ensuring that those who betray the public trust are held accountable.”

This case was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Shauna R. Prewitt, Sean Van Demark, and Bianca Calderon-Peñaloza.

Jesse Clark Garcia Age: 38 San Diego, CA

SUMMARY OF CHARGES

Conspiracy to Import Controlled Substances – Title 21, United States Code, Sections 952, 960, and 963

Maximum Penalty: Life in prison with a 10-year mandatory minimum

Importation of Controlled Substances – Title 21, United States Code, Sections 952 and 960

Maximum Penalty: Life in prison with a 10-year mandatory minimum

text:
The city of Salem isn’t at risk of harm from conditions to federal disaster relief funding asking local officials to reject diversity initiatives and support for immigrants, the Trump administration argued in court recently.

In a July 29 filing, an attorney for the federal government made the first rebuttal in court to the city’s lawsuit accusing authorities of withholding funding for flood damage repairs to force acceptance of President Donald Trump’s political agenda.

Federal attorneys Scott Bradford and Cameron Perla argued that the city does not face “irreparable” harm if it agrees to federal conditions for public assistance funding the city requested earlier this year. The city hasn’t proved it would suffer beyond “economic” harm, they wrote.

The city’s lawsuit, filed June 30 in Eugene U.S. District Court, names the Federal Emergency Management Agency and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, along with each agency’s top official.

READ IT: Salem v. FEMA, DHS

The funding, which is over $1 million, would go toward replacing culverts and repairing a roadway leading to the West Salem Sanitary Sewer Pump Station. The station pumps wastewater from West Salem to a treatment facility.

During intense flooding last December, the station experienced “catastrophic damage,” according to the city’s lawsuit.

Gov. Tina Kotek issued an emergency declaration in the following weeks and requested federal aid, which President Donald Trump approved in April. Kotek requested the aid go toward repairs for infrastructure damaged by the winter storm, including in Polk County.

Funding is first paid to state governments through FEMA’s Public Assistance Grant Program, and then amounts are distributed to smaller agencies, including the city of Salem.

City public works staff requested federal funding in early May, according to court filings. On May 26, state officials sent the grant agreement to city staff for signing.

The federal conditions at the center of Salem’s lawsuit are referenced by a link attachment at the end of the document.

The city’s suit describes the conditions as new, citing executive orders from Trump’s second term and updated grant conditions by DHS.

“These revisions, together with subsequent DHS actions and guidance, attempt to implement the current administration’s efforts to compel recipients (and their subrecipients) to abandon DEI policies despite clear statutory and decisional law that many such programs are lawful and to cease other activities that do not match the administration’s political agenda,” the lawsuit said.

Meanwhile, FEMA and DHS are arguing the conditions are not new and compliance with anti-discrimination laws has always been required for grant funding.

DHS’ standard grant conditions were last updated in April, according to the agency’s website.

They require that during the funding period, grant recipients “do not … operate any programs that advance or promote DEI, DEIA or discriminatory equity ideology” or “operate any program that benefits illegal immigrants or incentivizes illegal immigration.”

The federal government is also recommending the case be moved into the Court of Federal Claims, which oversees legal cases over issues including federal grants.

title: Column: Immigrant kids deserve to keep their lawyers - The Virginian-Pilot
description:
The Trump administration has jettisoned the way thousands of immigrant children receive legal help.
The Acacia Center for Justice was contracted by ORR to coordinate representation through a vast network of providers — lawyers, advocates, faith leaders and social workers.
HHS has refused to pay $65 million in overdue legal fees owed to the Acacia Center and its network of providers.
By Monday, one of the Acacia Center’s partners, the International Rescue Committee, announced it would continue to represent unaccompanied children in immigration court.
Abandoned and powerless children are not the “worst of the worst.” They deserve nurturing and compassion, not hate.
text:
The Trump administration has jettisoned the way thousands of immigrant children receive legal help. On July 31, the Department of Health and Human Services ended the contract with the Acacia Center for Justice after nearly two decades, leaving more than 20,000 unaccompanied kids in legal limbo.

Federal officials claim it’s a contract dispute. That’s a convenient excuse for their moral failure.

Federal immigration data shows that many of these children came to this country seeking refuge from harm. Some have been tortured and trafficked. Others were separated from their parents at the border. Most seek asylum, and many just want to be reunited with their families.

Congress recognized such trauma in 2008 when it passed the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act, which requires the HHS Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR) to provide legal representation for children navigating the immigration process. The Acacia Center for Justice was contracted by ORR to coordinate representation through a vast network of providers — lawyers, advocates, faith leaders and social workers.

But now this network clashes with what White House border czar Tom Homan calls its “deportation-maxxing” agenda. Although he promises to focus on arresting the “worst of the worst,” Homan’s strategy also involves targeting legal protections for vulnerable children so that the administration can accelerate their removal.

Administration officials have consistently defended child deportations by saying that “Children deserve to be with their parents.” They seem blind to the irony — that the Trump administration’s mass detention and deportation policies have separated more than 205,000 children from their parents as of May of this year, forcing thousands into detention or foster care.

HHS has refused to pay $65 million in overdue legal fees owed to the Acacia Center and its network of providers. The department says it’s withholding the money because the Acacia Center won’t turn over confidential information about its clients, including unredacted medical evaluations and details about their immigration cases. The center’s lawyers say that those demands force them to violate their attorney-client privilege and that the information has never been sought by any previous presidential administration — including during President Donald Trump’s first term.

HHS is also accusing the Acacia Center of fraud. Despite repeated questioning, however, HHS has provided no evidence to prove those fraud claims and, notably, makes the allegations exclusively in public statements, not in legal documents.

It’s all a smokescreen for the callous and calculated tactics HHS is employing. Since last September, the Department of Homeland Security has tried to coerce unaccompanied minor children to self-deport by telling them they could either give up their asylum claims and leave the country or face long-term detention.

The impact on the kids may be profound. Prolonged uncertainty “can really deepen anxiety, depression, post-traumatic stress, with consequences that extend well into adulthood,” Dr. C. Nicholas Cuneo, an assistant professor of Pediatrics and Medicine at the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine who works with refugees, told reporters on Friday.

But a trusted attorney “can buffer that harm,” he added, by helping children understand an incomprehensible process, giving them a safe and stable environment, and connecting them with healthcare, schools, housing and other support.

Congress has set aside money for the legal representation of unaccompanied minors, although it’s never been enough to meet the need. And the Trump administration has repeatedly shown it can find the money when the president wants to spend it. The $65 million in services rendered owed to the Acacia Center is far less than the $101 million in federal money spent on “beautification projects” to prepare Washington for the nation’s 250th anniversary celebration and the $600 million spent on a new White House ballroom.

By Monday, one of the Acacia Center’s partners, the International Rescue Committee, announced it would continue to represent unaccompanied children in immigration court. That’s promising, but it’s not sustainable.

Americans should be asking ourselves if we’re willing to scar a generation of young people so that this administration can pursue its anti-immigrant policies. Abandoned and powerless children are not the “worst of the worst.” They deserve nurturing and compassion, not hate.

Mary Ellen Klas is a politics and policy columnist for Bloomberg Opinion. A former capital bureau chief for the Miami Herald, she has covered politics and government for more than three decades.

title: Trump's latest swing at birthright citizenship might send issue back to courts
description:

The order trying to narrow birthright citizenship “is very unlikely to succeed,” says Nicole Hallett, director of the Immigrants’ Rights Clinic at the University of Chicago Law School.
For one, he says, it’s “long been accepted” that children of “alien enemies” aren’t entitled to birthright citizenship.
He directed federal agencies to withhold documents recognizing U.S. citizenship from people born under those circumstances.
Birth tourism Another order signed Thursday directs the Departments of State and Homeland Security to crack down on people or organizations suspected of enabling birth tourism.
text:
President Donald Trump is making a fresh attempt to limit birthright citizenship after losing on the issue at the U.S. Supreme Court in June.

A pair of executive orders signed Thursday take aim at specific groups of foreign parents. One tries to narrow automatic citizenship for children of parents with certain ties to foreign governments. The other directs a crackdown on what the administration defines as “birth tourism,” the practice of coming to the United States for the purpose of giving birth.

Legal experts question the legality of the president’s latest action in light of the Supreme Court’s rebuke, on constitutional grounds, of one of his past orders. They also expect more litigation against the White House, with a possible return to the nation’s top court.

The order trying to narrow birthright citizenship “is very unlikely to succeed,” says Nicole Hallett, director of the Immigrants’ Rights Clinic at the University of Chicago Law School. “The Supreme Court made it very clear that [Mr. Trump] did not have that power.”

Still, his executive action appears to signal that “the right is not going to give up this issue,” she says. “They view this as a generational fight.”

Others see more of an opening for the White House to get its way.

The latest actions by Mr. Trump “probe for weaknesses or open questions that remain” after the Supreme Court ruling in Trump v. Barbara earlier this summer, says Andrew Arthur, resident fellow in law and policy at the Center for Immigration Studies. For one, he says, it’s “long been accepted” that children of “alien enemies” aren’t entitled to birthright citizenship.

“There will be some very interesting cases that will come out of this,” Mr. Arthur says.

A Day 1 priority

Virtually everyone born in the United States is a U.S. citizen. Children of foreign diplomats are an exception.

On his first day back in office in January 2025, Mr. Trump signed an order that claimed automatic American citizenship didn’t extend to children born to parents in the U.S. unlawfully or temporarily, such as on a visa. He directed federal agencies to withhold documents recognizing U.S. citizenship from people born under those circumstances.

In June, the Supreme Court struck down that order, holding that the Constitution grants birthright citizenship to people born in the U.S. regardless of immigration status.

“We had a very unfortunate decision in the Supreme Court concerning birthright. ... So, we’re making adjustments,” Mr. Trump said at the White House on Thursday.

His latest order repackages his first, but this time targets children of immigrants deemed alien enemies, foreign government employees, and those who try to buy citizenship for their child, as well as children of noncitizens born in U.S. territories. The order claims to affect children not covered under the Supreme Court’s June decision.

Among other concerns, some legal experts point to the government’s broad discretion over who counts as an alien enemy. Those include “members” of foreign terror groups, Mr. Trump’s latest order notes. Last year, the White House used contested claims of terrorism ties to send Venezuelan men to a Salvadoran prison with little due process.

“Courts have shown incredible deference to the secretary of state's authority to designate foreign terrorist organizations,” says Wadie Said, a professor at the University of Colorado Law School. Though he doubts there are many members of those groups in the U.S., he says, Democratic and Republican administrations alike “have employed that trope for political purposes.”

While Mr. Trump has bashed birthright citizenship for more than a decade, most Americans support it, polling shows.

“If you really want to rewrite the birthright citizenship clause of the 14th Amendment, the best way is to rewrite” it, says Sandra Rierson, professor at Western State College of Law, though she doesn’t endorse the change. That would require a constitutional amendment.

Increasingly, some Republicans have argued that guaranteed citizenship at birth encourages not just illegal immigration, but “birth tourism” – a practice that is real but rare.

Birth tourism

Another order signed Thursday directs the Departments of State and Homeland Security to crack down on people or organizations suspected of enabling birth tourism. Mr. Trump defines that term as visa-holders entering the U.S. for the purpose of giving birth, or noncitizens assisting their entry.

While the birthright citizenship order appears to go “beyond what would be allowed by Trump v. Barbara,” the birth tourism executive order “doesn't seem like a wrong-headed or novel approach,” says Denise Gilman, director of the Immigration Clinic at the University of Texas School of Law. Birth tourism can – and should – be tackled through “regular visa issuance and enforcement,” she says.

It’s not illegal for foreigners to give birth in the United States. But lying in the visa application process about intentions for travel – such as if the goal is to give birth in the U.S. – is considered fraud.

Estimates of its prevalence vary.

As of 2024, the U.S. government reports around 3.6 million births a year, including some 9,600 births (less than 1%) to foreign residents in the U.S. and its territories. The Center for Immigration Studies, a think tank that favors restricted immigration, has estimated some 20,000 or more annual “birth tourists.”

The president’s order says birth tourism diverts consular resources away from “legitimate visa applicants,” and erodes public trust in the “faithful enforcement of the immigration laws.”

When challenging birthright citizenship before the Supreme Court, the government argument “focused quite a lot on birth tourism,” says Colleen Putzel-Kavanaugh, an associate policy analyst at the Migration Policy Institute.

Both directives signed by the president Thursday are broad, she says, with more changes likely to come as they are implemented.

“The devil is always in the details.”

text:
NEW JERSEY (PIX11) – Following a man’s death in the custody of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement at the immigration jail, Delaney Hall, New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport has announced a civil rights investigation into the facility’s practices.

According to a Friday afternoon announcement, Davenport launched an investigation into whether the detention center, owned and operated by The GEO Group, Inc., violated the civil rights of people detained there.

“New Jersey has a legal and a moral duty to stand up for the civil rights of people in our State,” said Attorney General Davenport. “For detained individuals, including those held by a private corporation like GEO Group, those rights include the right to humane treatment and adequate medical care. We will take every action available under law to safeguard these core legal principles. We ask individuals to share their personal experiences with us so that we can take action to ensure that rights are protected.”

At least two people have died at Delaney Hall.

In December, 41-year-old Haitian immigrant Jean Wilson Brutus passed away. Most recently, Edwin Lopez-Cornejo, a man from El Salvador, died at the beginning of August.

The death of Lopez-Cornejo has been labeled negligence by families and elected officials. His family says he was on medication for diabetes and high blood pressure and was not receiving the medical care he needed.

ICE has said Lopez-Cornejo “received proper medical care and was seen by medical professionals” while in custody. He had been held at the facility since his arrest on June 18, according to the agency, which accused him of entering the country illegally.

Lopez-Cornejo had lived in New Jersey for 20 years, according to his family.

The GEO Group is a private prison contractor that operates multiple detention centers across the country.

PIX11 News reached out to The GEO Group, which deferred us to ICE for comment. ICE was not immediately available to comment.

This story comprises reporting from The Associated Press, and PIX11 News reporters Emily Rahhal Geovany Dias, and Katie Corrado.

text:
Attorney General Jennifer Davenport announced Friday that the state has issued investigative subpoenas as part of a civil rights investigation into conditions at Delaney Hall, the embattled private immigration detention facility in Newark.

The investigation will examine whether Geo Group employees violated detainees’ civil rights, following mounting reports of poor conditions inside the facility and a string of detainee deaths reported in the last eight months.

“New Jersey has both a legal and a moral duty to stand up for the civil rights of people within our state,” Davenport said in a statement. “For people who are held involuntarily, including by a private corporation like Geo Group, those rights include the right to humane treatment and adequate medical care.”

The investigation comes less than a week after the death of Edwin Jovanny Lopez Cornejo, a 39-year-old Salvadorian who was held at Delaney Hall after he was arrested by federal immigration agents in June. His mother said in an interview that Cornejo was supposed to be taking daily medication for diabetes and high blood pressure, which he was not receiving at the jail. She noted that he complained of numbness in his face and hand when they last spoke. She learned of his death only when contacted by University Hospital to come identify his body on Aug. 1.

Officials with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement claim that Lopez Cornejo had received “proper medical care and was seen by medical professionals” while in custody. His official cause of death is pending.

The state Department of Health also confirmed the death of a third detainee connected to the facility, but has declined to release more information, citing pending investigations. Jean Wilson Brutus was the first reported death of a detainee at the jail in December 2025.

The 1,000-bed facility has drawn scrutiny since it opened in May 2025. Earlier this year, detainees said they launched a hunger and labor strike over conditions inside, which led to nightly clashes between federal agents and protesters along Doremus Avenue. Officials have also blocked the state from conducting a full health inspection inside.

Gov. Mikie Sherrill, a Democrat, said the civil rights investigation was necessary because of the stonewalling officials face at every turn.

“We’ve heard the reports of disturbing conditions and have been heartbroken by recent deaths of detainees at the facility. ICE and The Geo Group have continued to block our efforts for a full health inspection and there are now reports that visitations have been stopped,” she said in a statement.

Sherill repeated her position that Delaney Hall should be closed, and said her administration “will not tolerate a facility that abdicates any transparency and accountability.”

Spokespeople for Geo Group and the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond for comment.

If the investigation finds violations, the Attorney General’s Office said it would pursue civil enforcement action under the state Civil Rights Act and Law Against Discrimination. Officials are asking anyone with relevant information to contact the Affirmative Enforcement Unit.

text:
A North Carolina man has filed a claim seeking damages from the federal government, alleging he was arrested last year by immigration officers despite having valid REAL IDs, then dumped on the side of the road once the officers confirmed he was a U.S. citizen.

Viral cell phone video taken on November 18, 2025, by Fernando Vazquez Orea, an 18-year-old landscaper, showed Border Patrol agents uncuffing Vasquez in a wooded area. One of the officers throws Vasquez's ID and other papers out of an SUV, onto the ground, before driving off.

Now Vasquez, represented by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) of North Carolina, has filed a claim for damages under the Federal Tort Claims Act, a typical precursor to filing a civil lawsuit if the claim is ignored or denied by the government. Vasquez's claim alleges Border Patrol officers detained and handcuffed him during a warrantless construction site raid on November 18, 2025, and loaded him into an SUV, even though Vasquez provided the officers with his REAL ID.

"I am a hardworking blue-collar worker and landscaper," Vasquez said in an ACLU of North Carolina press release announcing the damages claim. "I plant trees, lay sod, and help improve the environment through my work. I have no criminal record, I graduated from high school, and I have goals like anyone else. One of my biggest goals is to start my own business and build a better future for myself and my family. On that eventful day, I believe I was targeted because of the color of my skin. I was handcuffed and placed in the back of an SUV, terrified and uncertain about what was going to happen next or whether I would still be able to achieve the goals I had worked so hard toward."

Vasquez is also one of five plaintiffs in a class action lawsuit filed by the ACLU of North Carolina challenging warrantless immigration arrests in the state.

Another of the plaintiffs in that suit, Willy Aceituno, was stopped by Customs and Border Protection agents in Charlotte last year but let go after he showed them his REAL ID. However, according to the lawsuit, after Aceituno started filming them on his phone, the agents shattered his truck window, threw him onto the pavement and broken glass, then drove him two miles away before leaving him on the side of the road, bleeding and disoriented.

"Mr. Vazquez and Mr. Aceituno's damages claims are part of a national effort to hold the federal government accountable and challenge the unlawful and abusive tactics that have harmed communities across our state and country," Corina Scott, a staff attorney at the ACLU of North Carolina, said in a press release. "North Carolinians have repeatedly witnessed and experienced these harms firsthand, and these claims are a meaningful step toward accountability and recourse."

According to the ACLU of North Carolina, Vasquez and Aceituno's claims are among 54 filed across 17 states and Washington, D.C., as part of a nationwide campaign challenging the Department of Homeland Security's (DHS) warrantless immigration stops.

Vasquez and Aceituno's claims are similar to those of scores of other U.S. citizens who say they've been detained, handcuffed, and in some cases assaulted by immigration officers. The Institute for Justice, a nonprofit public interest law firm, filed a lawsuit last year on behalf of Leo Garcia Venegas, an Alabama construction worker and U.S. citizen who has been detained and handcuffed three times by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers despite having a valid REAL ID on all three occasions. The law firm is also representing George Retes, a U.S. citizen and Army veteran, who was tear-gassed and jailed for three days last July during an immigration raid in California. ProPublica identified at least 170 Americans who'd been detained by ICE in an investigation published last October.

The DHS has argued in court filings and testimony in Venegas' case that REAL IDs aren't reliable confirmation of citizenship, even though federal law requires states to verify citizenship before issuing them, and even though the DHS is the agency responsible for ensuring state compliance with the law.

The DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

However, in previous statements to Reason, the DHS has repeatedly said that "allegations that DHS law enforcement engages in 'racial profiling' are disgusting, reckless, and categorically FALSE. What makes someone a target for immigration enforcement is if they are illegally in the U.S.—NOT their skin color, race, or ethnicity."

"DHS is NOT arresting U.S. citizens by mistake," the statements continued. "DHS enforcement operations are highly targeted, and officers do their due diligence. We know who we are targeting ahead of time. If and when we do encounter individuals subject to arrest, our law enforcement is trained to ask a series of well-determined questions to determine status and removability."

Nevertheless, those statements don't account for how citizens like Vasquez ended up on the side of the road.

"The entire experience left me feeling powerless, frightened, humiliated, and deeply shaken," Vasquez said. "It has had a lasting emotional impact on me. I believe what happened to me was unjust, and I am seeking accountability and justice for what I experienced. I want my story to be heard so that no one else has to go through what I experienced."

The New Jersey Division on Civil Rights issued subpoenas to determine whether employees of the privately owned immigration detention facility violated the civil rights of immigrants in detention. The investigation comes shortly after a Salvadoran man, Edwin Lopez-Cornejo , died after facing a medical emergency while being detained at the facility.

The facility, based in Newark, has been under intense scrutiny after it reopened during the second Trump administration. The GEO Group, one of the country’s largest private detention companies, operates the detention facility under a $1 billion contract that lasts for 15 years. The facility has 1,000 beds.

Former detainees at the facility have described squalid conditions — including substandard food and difficulty accessing medical care. The Trump administration and GEO Group have denied claims of substandard care.

“New Jersey has both a legal and a moral duty to stand up for the civil rights of people within our state,” state Attorney General Jennifer Davenport said in a statement. “For people who are held involuntarily, including by a private corporation like GEO Group, those rights include the right to humane treatment and adequate medical care. We will take every action available under law to safeguard these core legal principles. We ask individuals to share their personal experiences with us so that we can take action to ensure that rights are protected.”

The Department of Homeland Security and GEO Group did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Located in an industrial part of North Jersey, the immigration jail has become a political flashpoint as tensions over immigration policy continue to rise. Protestors clashed with federal agents outside the facility in May, leading to Gov. Mikie Sherrill to send in state police. Seperately, the mayor of Newark was arrested during a chaotic scrum outside the jail last year. While the charges against the mayor were dropped, Rep. LaMonica McIver (D-N.J.) was eventually charged with assaulting law enforcement stemming from that scuffle — charges she is still fighting today.

The Sherrill administration sued GEO Group seeking to give state health inspectors full access to the facility. That lawsuit is ongoing.

“We will not tolerate a facility that abdicates any transparency and accountability,” Sherrill said in a statement. “I have long opposed private detention facilities, and my position is clear that Delaney Hall should be closed. My administration will continue to do everything in our power to hold ICE and The GEO Group accountable to New Jersey laws.”

text:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

August 7, 2026

MEDIA CONTACTS

IRAP | Spencer Tilger | media@refugeerights.org

AALDEF | Stuart J. Sia | media@aaldef.org

FEDERAL COURT ALLOWS TERMINATION OF TPS TO PROCEED FOR NEARLY 4,000 PEOPLE FROM BURMA

“I am devastated by the court’s ruling and terrified of what will happen if I’m forced to return to Burma”

(Chicago, IL) — Today, a federal court declined to extend emergency relief for nearly 4,000 TPS holders from Burma, a devastating decision that will allow the Trump administration to begin deporting Burmese TPS holders who lack other legal status. The court’s ruling allows the administration to proceed with ending TPS protections for Burmese nationals and permits further litigation only on the claim that the TPS termination was unconstitutionally discriminatory.

“I am devastated by the court’s ruling and terrified of what will happen if I’m forced to return to Burma,” said Thura Doe, a plaintiff in the lawsuit. “As an advocate for democracy in Burma, I have vocally protested the current military dictatorship in my home country. If I am forced to return, I deeply fear I will be immediately detained by the junta—which is what I’ve witnessed happen to friends, many who remain imprisoned by the military dictatorship.”

“This court was the only thing standing between thousands of our Burmese clients and the Trump administration’s mass detention-and-deportation machine,” said Lupe Aguirre, Deputy Director of U.S. Litigation at the International Refugee Assistance Project (IRAP). “But with this decision, the termination of TPS for Burma is in effect. TPS holders deserve better than a government that flagrantly violates the law and courts that are powerless to stop it. TPS holders need a permanent fix and protection from being sent to danger. Congress must act now to extend protections for all TPS holders.”

Last month, following the Supreme Court’s decision in Mullin v. Doe, IRAP, Asian American Legal Defense and Education Fund (AALDEF), and the Law Offices of June J. Htun, sought renewed emergency relief to pause the termination of TPS, arguing that the administration’s actions were unlawful violations of the due process clause and the authority Congress delegated to the Department of Homeland Security. The court declined to grant emergency relief and dismissed both new claims.

As a result of today’s court ruling, nearly 4,000 Burmese TPS holders who have lived in the United States for years will no longer have TPS protections while this lawsuit proceeds.

“The court’s decision to allow TPS protections to lapse puts thousands of Burmese TPS holders in grave danger. It is unconscionable for the Trump administration to gamble with their lives as part of its larger campaign to use immigration policy as a tool for racial exclusion,” said Dinesh McCoy, staff attorney at AALDEF, lead counsel in the case. “We are continuing to explore all available legal options. Regardless of the outcome of the litigation, our work will not end. We will continue to pursue every available avenue to protect and advocate for affected communities.”

TPS is a humanitarian program established by Congress that allows individuals from designated countries experiencing armed conflict, natural disasters, or other extraordinary and unsafe conditions to live and work legally in the United States. Burma remains engulfed in violent conflict following the 2021 military coup, widespread human rights abuses, and unsafe conditions exacerbated by a 7.7 magnitude earthquake earlier this year. The U.S. State Department continues to warn Americans against travel to Burma due to extreme danger.

“The court’s ruling today is heartbreaking and will have deeply harmful human consequences,” said June Htun, an attorney on the case. “The Trump administration did not afford people the protections that should have been required by Congress and the Constitution. With Burma still mired in civil war, sending TPS holders back to the country will literally put their lives at risk.”

AALDEF serves diverse Asian communities around the country in solidarity with each other, communities of color, and marginalized groups. Community lawyering is at the heart of AALDEF’s work, which combines litigation, advocacy, education, and organizing to secure human rights for all people.

text:
Attorney General Jennifer Davenport has opened a civil rights investigation into Delaney Hall, escalating the state’s battle with the private immigration detention facility following reports of troubling conditions and several detainee deaths.

The New Jersey Division on Civil Rights has issued investigative subpoenas to determine whether actions or inaction by employees of The GEO Group, which owns and operates the Newark facility, violated detainees’ rights.

“New Jersey has both a legal and a moral duty to stand up for the civil rights of people within our state,” Davenport said. “For people who are held involuntarily, including by a private corporation like GEO Group, those rights include the right to humane treatment and adequate medical care. We will take every action available under law to safeguard these core legal principles. We ask individuals to share their personal experiences with us so that we can take action to ensure that rights are protected.”

Gov. Mikie Sherrill, who has called for Delaney Hall to close, said GEO Group and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement have blocked the state’s attempts to inspect the facility.

“Today, the Attorney General announced a civil rights investigation into Delaney Hall, a private detention facility operated by The GEO Group.” Sherrill stated. “Since the facility is stonewalling efforts for real oversight, this is the right and necessary course of action.

Sherrill pointed to reports of “disturbing conditions” and said she’s been “heartbroken by recent deaths of detainees at the facility.”

“ICE and The GEO Group have continued to block our efforts for a full health inspection, and there are now reports that visitations have been stopped. We will not tolerate a facility that abdicates any transparency and accountability. I have long opposed private detention facilities, and my position is clear that Delaney Hall should be closed.” She said. “My administration will continue to do everything in our power to hold ICE and The GEO Group accountable to New Jersey laws.”

The investigation comes as litigation continues between the Department of Health and GEO Group. Davenport filed a lawsuit on behalf of the department in June seeking a court order requiring the company to admit state health inspectors.

If investigators uncover violations, the Attorney General’s Office could pursue civil enforcement under the New Jersey Civil Rights Act and the state Law Against Discrimination.

“Ensuring that civil rights are upheld in all environments — particularly in settings where individuals may be vulnerable — is a fundamental responsibility,” said Yolanda Melville, the Division on Civil Rights director. “Our investigation will be thorough, impartial, and guided by the requirements and protections established by New Jersey law.”

The division is asking detainees, employees and others with relevant information to contact its Affirmative Enforcement Unit.
