text:
When Dilmer “Loba” Lovos Mendez learned about the protests inside the Dilley Detention Center in Texas, they were not surprised. While being held for two years in California immigration jails from 2024 to 2026, Lovos Mendez had seen firsthand how common such organized acts of resistance actually are, and was themself directly involved with three protest actions during that time.

During two hunger strikes, one of which had up to 100 participants, as well as sit-ins that lasted two weeks in September 2025, Lovos Mendez worked with other people inside immigrant jails to protest medical neglect and terrible conditions including rotten food and undrinkable water.

As in the case of Dilley, Lovos Mendez felt it was outrageous that the detainees had to be the ones to expose conditions and make people aware. “It’s the only way that a person inside the detention center can actually have their voices heard,” Lovos Mendez told Truthout.

During the same month as the sit-ins that Lovos Mendez participated in at California City Immigration Processing Center, hunger strikes emerged at Louisiana State Prison (also known as Angola, for the slave plantation it was built over) in “Camp 57,” a solitary confinement unit that was housing immigrants in federal custody. Detainees were given small “childlike” portions of food and weren’t allowed to go to commissary, on top of being housed in tiny cells meant for solitary confinement, according to Chanthila Souvannarath, who helped lead the hunger strike from inside.

“We wanted to expose the corruption,” Souvannarath told Truthout. “It’s not a place for detainees. We’re trying to get that place shut down. It’s inhumane.”

These were just two of the many protests emerging in immigration jails across the U.S., only a few of which have come into the national spotlight under the second Trump administration. Even so, Alex Mensing, who works with the California Collaborative for Immigrant Justice, told Truthout that protests happen inside immigration jails all the time, even if it is just one person leading a hunger strike from solitary confinement. These facilities have been sites of resistance since their inception, with one of the first recorded protests occurring in 1985 in El Centro Detention Facility in California.

“There’s a very long lineage and history of incarcerated people resisting as a form of survival, very much as a form of political activism once they’re incarcerated, and sometimes they work with people on the outside in solidarity, but still very much motivated by the people on the inside themselves,” said Jessica Ordaz, a historian and assistant professor of ethnic studies at the University of Colorado Boulder.

Under-Documented Protests

Ordaz told Truthout that when she began researching El Centro Detention Facility, which was built in the 1940s and closed in 2014, she wasn’t trying to look at examples of protests or resistance, but that was the story she found.

She began researching hunger strikes in El Centro that happened in 1985 with about 300 participants. The protest ended after the number of strikers dwindled over several days and guards went in with riot gear, forcibly moved the remaining protestors, and force-fed them. However, when Ordaz interviewed people about that incident, they’d bring up other protests that happened inside the facility.

“They were like, ‘Oh yeah, there was one in ’84 and ’83,’” Ordaz said.

She realized the number of protests occurring was far higher than what had been documented.

“I don’t know the number, but I will say I generally did see a pattern of them happening very frequently,” Ordaz said. “Unless there’s hundreds and hundreds of incarcerated folks involved, sometimes it’s not picked up [by the media].”

Mensing agreed. As communications director with the California Collaborative for Immigrant Justice, which communicates with immigrants in custody to support their cases and document abuse, he frequently hears about protests happening inside immigration jails in California. Mensing estimated that hundreds of protests have occurred inside since Trump started his second term. He said that most of these protests are sit-ins, shape formations, and hunger strikes — but they only get covered if hundreds of people participate, while smaller ones often fly under the radar.

“We never hear about everything that happens inside, and there’s a lot of protest that goes on, sometimes even on a daily basis, just for people to get the basics,” Mensing said.

The California Collaborative for Immigrant Justice counts a hunger strike even if only one person is involved. If one person does three hunger strikes, then that is already three protests at one detention center in one year. Mensing documented dozens in California detention centers already during the first three months of 2026.

“Multiply that by the number of detention centers, it’s going to be a lot,” Mensing said.

Fighting for Basic Needs

Mensing said that oftentimes incarcerated immigrants use these protests to secure very basic needs like medication, proper food, medical attention, help with their cases, or ways to combat extreme heat. Ordaz has seen the same patterns in her studies of protests in decades past.

“It’s the same story happening decade after decade in terms of the maltreatment and the abuses inside,” Ordaz said.

For Lovos Mendez, who was deported to El Salvador in March, their advocacy in immigrant detention centers started as soon as they arrived at Golden State Annex in California in 2024. They immediately noticed detainees not being given their medication, being served moldy food, and getting sent to solitary confinement for not following orders, despite language barriers. In February 2024, they began working with others inside to plan a hunger strike that took place in April 2024 and garnered nearly 100 participants. The effort was supported by the California Collaborative for Immigrant Justice.

“We conducted these hunger strikes to stand up for our rights, especially with the food and the medical services,” Lovos Mendez said. “It was a community thing. We all came collectively after seeing so many people suffering from illnesses and health issues that needed medications, and we’re not being given them.”

Another hunger strike took place after that one. Lovos Mendez and many others faced retaliation, including solitary confinement, force feeding, and delayed medications. Lovos Mendez was transferred to the California City Detention Center, a relocation which they saw as a form of retaliation for having demonstrated for human rights. The move positioned them hours away, where it became harder for their mother to visit them.

“The retaliation was to be expected from them, however, we were not prepared for the form of retaliation when they started separating us from our peers, and they started transferring people, little by little disintegrating the coalition that we had formed in order for us to be able to demand fair treatment,” Lovos Mendez said.

Solidarity With Outside Organizers

When Rebecca Asaki, an organizer with Tsuru for Solidarity, a Japanese American organization made up of survivors of U.S. internment camps during World War II and their descendants, heard about the children protesting in the Dilley Detention Center in January, she thought of the 2015 hunger strike led by mothers in Dilley before the facility closed down the first time. The action was coordinated with Tsuru and other organizations as part of a coalition to end family detention, which won an ultimately temporary victory in 2021.

During that time, the coalition also organized other inside and outside actions, including campaigning for the release of Haitian families detained inside the Berks County Residential Center in 2020, before it closed down in 2023.

“We had Haitian drums and Japanese drums, and we were singing,” Asaki said. “The folks who were detained inside also came out cheering us on as we were cheering them on. It was a really incredible moment where we were simultaneously able to have actions.”

Asaki said it is important to have people organizing on the outside to uplift the actions happening inside. She also said that Tsuru’s actions are guided by people who are or were in immigration detention.

Similarly, Josefina Mora Chung has been uplifting protests inside the Tacoma Northwest Detention Center with La Resistencia, which was founded 22 years ago to help people on hunger strikes in immigration jails get their demands out. One thousand two hundred people participated in the 2014 hunger strike at Tacoma Northwest Detention Center, and some of them reached out to the La Resistencia founder to ask for help amplifying their message. That hunger strike lasted for 50 days.

To Mora Chung, the detainees’ outreach demonstrated that there was a large need for outside organizers to step in. “People in detention were asking for a lot more support and in their efforts to pressure for the closure of this particular facility, we began running concurrent campaigns on the outside to create outside pressure, as well as organize with people inside to aim for the eventual closure of this facility,” Mora Chung told Truthout.

Mora Chung said La Resistencia has documented about a dozen hunger strikes in the Tacoma Northwest Detention Center every year of its 12-year existence. Last year, La Resistencia documented 16 hunger strikes. By May of this year the group had already documented 13.

Resistance inside immigration jails is widespread. But robust solidarity efforts on the outside, which organizers like Mora Chung see as essential to the success of inside protests, are significantly rarer.

text:
The Trump administration must immediately reimburse legal aid groups for services they provided to unaccompanied migrant children under a now-expired government contract, a federal trial court judge ruled.

The ruling sides with a coalition of nonprofits who claimed that the Trump administration was violating a court order by demanding additional information in order to pay out more than $65 million billed since December. The administration argued it had the right to withhold payment until it has what it needed to validate the invoices, citing accounting concerns with the contractors.

The US District Court for the Northern District of California ordered the Department of Health and Human Services to disburse the funding by Friday so it can be in compliance with an April 2025 preliminary injunction requiring continued funding for the program.

“Defendants’ ongoing conditioning of disbursement of required funding inevitably results in ‘cutting off access to congressionally appropriated funding’ for ‘direct legal representation services to unaccompanied children,’” Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín said late Thursday. “This violates both the plain language as well as the spirit of the preliminary injunction.”

HHS had provided funding to Acacia Center for Justice and over 80 subcontracted nonprofits since 2023 to provide representation and know-your-rights training to migrant children with immigration court hearings. In March 2025, the Trump administration issued stop work orders in an attempt to end the contract backing that funding, spurring a multi-group lawsuit.

Data Sharing Dispute

The plaintiffs — consisting of over a dozen groups who were subcontractors until the pact expired July 31st — claimedthe Trump administration conditioned funding based on whether the groups would be willing to provide case information that would violate attorney-client privilege.

The Justice Department said the requested information doesn’t violate attorney-client privilege and is necessary to substantiate the groups’ billing.

Martínez-Olguín noted that the government’s substantiation argument has been rejected various times by the court.

“In so arguing, Defendants tie themselves in a knot — despite their insistence that this Court lacks jurisdiction over the government’s contractual disputes, they now attempt to utilize a contractual dispute as a shield for their failure to abide by the terms of the preliminary injunction,” her order said.

New Contractor

The court order also requires HHS to file a report by Aug. 13 detailing their efforts to provide migrant child legal services through new contractors.

The decision was issued two days after the the Trump administration announced a proposed $150 million no-bid cooperative agreement with Burke Law Group—a 26-person firm based in Houston that has ties to the Trump administration and specializes in environmental law and white collar crime.

The plaintiff organizations noted in a recent brief that the government gave them a 120-day transition period to transfer cases for clients currently staying in Office of Refugee Resettlement shelters. The legal aid providers are “operating in the dark” as they wait for more information about the transition process, Wendy Young, the executive director of former subcontractor Kids in Need of Defense, said ahead of the hearing.

“There’s no plan in place yet for the transfer and transition of the 25,000ish cases that are exist under the current contract, Young said. “So it could be that Burke Law Group is expected to take all of those, some of those, or none of those. We don’t know yet.”

The administration offered some additional details on the future of the program in a declaration filed to the court by Richard Debany, the ORR’s chief for division of acquisition requirements. The agency offered Acacia “a four-month bridge arrangement” to facilitate the transition process, while reaching a $20 million cooperative agreement with a different nonprofit to assist with migrant child legal services, according to Debany.

An ORR spokesperson said in an emailed statement that “details regarding this work are procurement sensitive but will be shared once a contract is formally secured.”

“ORR is committed to ensuring every UAC has legal representation in immigration court, which is why ORR began using the U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants (USCRI) to provide legal representation to all UAC in ORR care on August 5th.”

Gibson Dunn & Crutcher LLP, the Justice Action Center, Immigrant Defenders Law Center, and in-house attorneys for the Amica Center represent the plaintiffs.

text:
Justice William Paterson is, to date, the only justice to have been born in Ireland and is one of only six justices to have been born outside of the United States.

Paterson was born in December 1745 in County Antrim. In 1747, before he turned two, the family left for America and arrived in Delaware. His father sold tin goods throughout the colonies before opening a general store in Princeton in 1750, across the road from the soon-to-be-built Nassau Hall, today the oldest building at Princeton University (and which served as a battleground during the American Revolution). Aided by local real-estate purchases, Paterson’s father was able to fund his son’s education. Admitted to the College of New Jersey (today Princeton University) at 14, Paterson helped establish the Cliosophic Society with Aaron Burr, a “social and debating club” whose name he likely coined. After graduating in 1763 and earning a graduate degree three years later, he read law under Richard Stockton and was admitted to the bar in 1768.

After the American Revolution began, Paterson served as a delegate to and secretary of New Jersey’s provincial congresses, recording the state’s first official constitution in 1776, while also serving as an officer in the Somerset County Minutemen and on the Council of Safety, which organized New Jersey’s militia. As the state’s first attorney general from 1776 to 1783, Paterson “actively prosecuted Loyalists” while also maintaining a busy private practice. Tragically, his infant daughter died in June 1783 and his wife Cornelia passed away that November, four days after the birth of their son.

The Constitutional Convention proved Paterson’s “finest hour.” According to fellow delegate William Pierce, Paterson was “one of those kind of Men whose powers break in upon you, and create wonder and astonishment.” Championing the small states, Paterson introduced the New Jersey Plan (sometimes known as the Paterson Plan), proposing a one-chamber legislature where every state would vote as an equal. A week after the “Great Compromise” established equal state representation in the Senate – two members per state, protecting small states, to balance against another chamber with proportional representation – Paterson departed the Convention on July 23, leaving the drafting to others. He reappeared in September to sign the Constitution, becoming one of seven foreign-born signers.

Elected to the first Senate, Paterson drafted the Judiciary Act of 1789 alongside his old Princeton classmate (and future chief justice) Oliver Ellsworth, which set the initial number of justices on the Supreme Court at six. Indeed, the act’s first nine sections (which created the district and circuit courts, among other things) are in Paterson’s handwriting. Paterson then became the first person ever to resign from the Senate, trading his seat to become the second governor of New Jersey.

President George Washington nominated Paterson to the Supreme Court in 1793 but withdrew the nomination the next day over a procedural issue. Washington then renominated him on March 4 and he was confirmed that same day. (Washington later offered him the role of Secretary of State in 1795, which Paterson declined.)

One of Paterson’s most important statements came while riding circuit, in 1795’s Vanhorne’s Lessee v. Dorrance, where his jury charge asked “What is a Constitution? It is the form of government, delineated by the mighty hand of the people.” He continued that “every act of the Legislature, repugnant to the Constitution, is absolutely void” – which Chief Justice John Marshall drew on in Marbury v. Madison. In 1796’s Hylton v. United States, Paterson wrote that the carriage tax (a federal tax on carriages kept for the owner's personal use, passed by Congress in 1794) was “indirect,” meaning it could stand under the Constitution. Two years later in Calder v. Bull, Paterson joined three colleagues in a unanimous judgment (only four justices heard the case and each wrote a seriatim opinion) confining ex post facto clauses – which prevent Congress and the states from passing laws that reach backward onto past conduct – to criminal laws only.

description:
(Disclaimer : I know I’ve already riled up a bunch of people just by bringing up the island nation.
The island nation has been plagued by power outages over the last two years, caused by mechanical failures, damage from severe storms and fuel shortages.
The U.S. embargo against Cuba goes back over 60 years, to when Castro seized power by ousting the U.S.-backed leader, Fulgencio Batista, in the late 1950s.
All these years later, the U.S. stubbornly is standing by Red Scare ideologies to rationalize the embargo.
Having recently gone to the Caribbean nation, Schlenker saw firsthand the devastating effects of how badly the U.S. is choking out the country.
text:
Let’s talk about Cuba.

(Disclaimer : I know I’ve already riled up a bunch of people just by bringing up the island nation. So I want to make something very clear: I am going to be talking about the people living in Cuba with respect and empathy. If you were looking for me to rant about Fidel Castro, communism and other Cold War-era talking points, you must have me confused with Marco Rubio.)

Over the weekend, Cuba suffered yet another nationwide blackout, which came only a few weeks after it was hit with three blackouts in nine days in July.

The island nation has been plagued by power outages over the last two years, caused by mechanical failures, damage from severe storms and fuel shortages.

But the situation has been greatly exacerbated by the United States.

Venezuela had long been a provider of oil and fuel to Cuba, but after the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, the U.S. took control of the South American country’s oil reserves. President Trump also threatened to impose tariffs on countries that send oil to the island.

The U.S. embargo against Cuba goes back over 60 years, to when Castro seized power by ousting the U.S.-backed leader, Fulgencio Batista, in the late 1950s. The fear of communism somehow hopping from the island to the U.S. set in stateside and was further bolstered by the fact that the Soviet Union began backing Cuba. Insert the Bay of Pigs invasion, the nuclear arms race and the other stuff you probably (hopefully) learned about in school — and that’s how we got to the current situation.

All these years later, the U.S. stubbornly is standing by Red Scare ideologies to rationalize the embargo.

Relations with Cuba have further worsened under the Trump and Biden administrations. In 2017 and 2019, the Trump administration severely restricted the flow of tourism to the island with the Cuba Restricted List: an ever-expanding registry of Cuban businesses — largely tourism-based institutions such as hotels — that Americans were prohibited from doing business with.

That list was further expanded last year at the start of the second Trump administration. The U.S. also banned all cruise ships from going to Cuba beginning in 2019.

The U.S. had further disincentivized businesses and financial institutions from operating in Cuba when it deemed the Caribbean country a state sponsor of terrorism in 2021, a distinction Cuba shares with North Korea, Iran and Syria.

Changes in import legislation imposed by the U.S. have led to a lack of access to medical tools and medications in Cuba. Because of this, more than 50% of medications on the island are in short supply.

Restrictions on remittances also have limited the amount of aid Cubans can receive from family members and charitable organizations from the States. This lack of funds, in turn, leaves families without the ability to purchase necessities.

“I would argue that a war with Cuba has already begun,” said Lee Schlenker — a research associate at the trans-partisan political “action tank” and communications project called the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft.

“It’s very difficult for the over 9 million Cubans who are just coming out from the sixth nationwide blackout to argue that this administration’s indiscriminate war against the island’s economy hasn’t already begun,” he told The Times. “[Cubans] believe mostly that things will only get worse before they get better.”

But why has the U.S. decided to ramp up its offensive against Cuba over the last few months? Look no further than son of Cuban exiles and current secretary of State: Rubio.

“This is really a pet project of Marco Rubio,” Schlenker said. “The operation to extract Nicolas Maduro in Venezuela was very clearly aimed at destabilizing Cuba through cutting off oil sales. Rubio was the architect of the 2017 national security presidential memorandum that reversed the Obama administration’s historic détente with the island, despite the objections of basically all of the first Trump administration’s deputies in all of the major cabinets.

“He’s always been beholden to a small group of powerful and influential Americans in South Florida,” Schlenker added. “[He’s] a hawkish neoconservative who believes that we must export human rights and democracy, allegedly, whether through force, through coercion or diplomatic arm twisting.”

Cuba is a boogeyman character for Rubio. There’s nothing he’d want more than to bring down the Cuban government to heel and tout that as a victory — in spite of all the Cuban people who would be endangered by that.

This is all part of the larger “Don-roe Doctrine,” in which the U.S. looks to justify its interference with all governments in the Western Hemisphere.

Having recently gone to the Caribbean nation, Schlenker saw firsthand the devastating effects of how badly the U.S. is choking out the country.

“People are tired, they’re exhausted. There’s really no hope,” he said. “People don’t even know who to blame anymore. They know that Trump is to blame, that they have their hands tied. They don’t really see a way out.”

I too would be hard-pressed to see a way out if I was living in complete darkness, if I needed to wait weeks for a necessary surgery, if my children were on the brink of starvation, if I saw the other nations were too scared of the U.S. to send aid, if infant mortality rates were skyrocketing and cancer survival rates were plummeting.

What would the Cuban people have to look forward to if the U.S. was able to swing its political power within the country? Let’s just look at Venezuela.

The U.S. was able to go in and extradite Maduro and have Delcy Rodríguez play the part of puppet — they didn’t even install Trump’s populist political buddy, María Corina Machado, after the takeover. Venezuela has lost control of its valuable resources and has yet to benefit from the U.S. intervention.

You’d think the U.S. would have a vested interest in helping move along Venezuela’s recovery process after twin earthquakes devastated the country in late June, which resulted in more than 6,000 deaths. But that hasn’t been the case.

“Venezuela has crucial resources that it is not being allowed to access. The United States and Europe are blocking the nation from more than $11 billion that Venezuela should legally have,” Mark Weisbrot, the co-director of the Center for Economic and Policy Research, recently wrote in a column for The Times.

“There are some billions of dollars more that are being held by the Trump administration, despite an executive order stating that these funds ‘constitute property of the Government of Venezuela.’ This is cash from the sale of Venezuela’s oil, which the Trump administration has taken control.”

But why does all this matter to Latinos in the U.S.? Well, it reflects this administration’s views of Latinos.

We are resources and political tools to the government — nothing more. Just chess pieces that are used to gain imperialistic points.

Whether Latinos live or die is not of importance to the U.S. political machine; it’s obvious.

Create an unstable situation that makes life unmanageable and then demonize the victims of that situation when they ask you for help — that’s the U.S. government’s MO.

Last year, the Trump administration terminated Temporary Protected Status for 600,000 Venezuelans, making them all eligible for removal from the country. That ruling also stripped away protections for thousands of Cuban in the U.S.

Today’s Venezuelan earthquake and Cuban blackout victims are tomorrow’s Immigration and Customs Enforcement detainees.

Remembering the El Paso shooting

On Aug. 3, 2019, a gunman drove more than nine hours from North Texas to an El Paso Walmart and killed 23 people while injuring 22 others. The assailant later admitted to authorities that the attack was racially motivated against Latinos.

The shooter is facing 23 life sentences for his crimes, and the families of the dead must face every day without their loved ones.

Over the last week, vigils for the victims have been held at memorial sites throughout the Texas city.

“It was not only Walmart, it was our community at the border that was attacked. Violently,” an immigration reform and human rights advocate told El Paso NBC affiliate KTSM. “So yes, we need to remember each of them. But at the same time we need to remember, and not forget, the ideas, the narrative behind that attack.”

Seven years after the shooting, I wish I could say I feel more hopeful that something like this never will happen again, but I really can’t.

Latino hate crimes are up across the nation, reaching record highs last year, and Latinos continually have been shot and killed in the streets by government officials over the last few years. Thousands more Latino men, women and children have been locked up and forced to live in rundown, disease-and-vermin-filled detention centers.

Gun laws continue to remain loose throughout the majority of the country, especially in Texas. Just this week, a Texas judge passed a ruling that could allow firearm owners to purchase firearm suppressors and other firearms without registration, while also removing a layer of background checks.

What a messed-up country we live in.

text:
WASHINGTON — New Jersey’s two U.S. senators on Friday launched a new effort to increase oversight of Delaney Hall following the death of detainee Edwin Lopez-Cornejo.

U.S. Sens. Cory Booker and Andy Kim proposed taking using about $115 million from the $2.5 billion Immigration and Customs Enforcement budget to reopen the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s Office of the Immigration Detention Ombudsman, a watchdog agency Congress created years earlier but was shut down by President Donald Trump’s administration in May. The allocation would fund the ombudsman’s office for four years.

The resurrected office would investigate complaints and allegations of misconduct, and make recommendations to improve conditions for those being held in detention facilities.

It also would oversee private contractors working for ICE, such as the Geo Group that runs Delaney Hall. If the ombudsman finds that those contractors have violated federal law or detention standards, the legislation would cut off payments until they make changes required by the office.

“For too long, private detention contractors have operated with too little accountability and too little oversight,” Booker said. “When facilities violate standards, use excessive force, or fail to provide humane conditions, there must be real consequences.”’

The bill is the latest effort by New Jersey Democratic lawmakers outraged by the recent death of Lopez-Cornejo, 41, a Salvadoran national, who was the third person to die at the Newark detention center in less than a year. Booker went to the Senate floor Thursday in an unsuccessful effort to pass legislation closing Delaney Hall, and the nine House Democrats from the Garden State sent a letter to the heads of DHS and ICE, demanding answers about the deaths of the three detainees and the medical care being provided to those in the Newark facility.

Congress created the ombudsman office in 2019 to address the treatment and care of immigrants during Trump’s first term, but his administration began shrinking it at the start of his second term as it ratcheted up its enforcement of immigration laws. The administration closed the office completely in May.

The senators pointed out that at least 56 people have died in ICE custody since January 2025 and more than 70% of those detained by the agency have no criminal convictions.

text:
Officers for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) will be equipped with much-delayed body cameras by the end of next month, it was reported on Friday. But experts have questioned the transparency of a policy that allows the ICE director to restrict the public release of footage unless “it is in the best interests of the agency”.

Pressure has mounted on the Trump administration to provide body cameras after people caught up in encounters with federal immigration personnel suffered death or serious injuries.

Two men were shot and killed by ICE agents, in Texas and Maine, last month in circumstances similar to the death of another man during a traffic stop in Illinois last September. None of the officers involved was wearing a camera.

Tom Homan, Trump’s so-called border czar, said last month that ICE officers would be required to have at least one body camera recording during future vehicle stops. Policy for body-worn cameras was first established in a February 2025 ICE directive, but funding for their provision was held up by this year’s partial government shutdown, Homan said.

The intention of using such cameras, according to David Venturella, the ICE acting director, is to increase transparency and accountability.

One analyst, however, told the Associated Press that an accompanying “selective release” policy of footage meant taxpayers who put up more than $30m for the cameras may still be kept in the dark about some high-profile confrontations, at least in their immediate aftermath.

Christopher Schneider, a sociology professor at Canada’s Brandon University, and co-author of Police Body-Worn Cameras: Media and the New Discourse of Police Reform, said the ICE director would have discretion to release recordings that reflect well on the agency’s image while working to keep others secret.

“In some ways, ICE is saying the quiet part out loud,” he said. “Body-worn cameras are being used as contemporary image-work tools to present the police to the public in the most favorable way possible.”

The policy says ICE will promptly release video of shootings and other encounters in which its agents cause death or serious injury only after determining “it is in the best interests of the agency” to do so.

It requires officers to activate cameras during routine enforcement activities, including while making arrests, executing search warrants and responding to emergencies.

After shootings or other serious confrontations, a committee that includes top ICE officials and lawyers will review footage and recommend whether to release it promptly, according to the February 2025 policy.

If the ICE director finds that “specific and compelling circumstances” justify withholding the video, they have the authority to block or indefinitely delay the release, the policy says.

The Trump administration slow-walked a pilot program last year to provide cameras to ICE personnel, it was reported in January, and moved to cut funding.

Civilian cellphone footage of the deaths of protesters Renee Good and Alex Pretti at the hands of federal immigration officers in separate January incidents in Minneapolis allowed their families and supporters to challenge authorities’ accounts of the encounters.

Homan, in a TV appearance on Fox & Friends last month, said he welcomed the imminent rollout of the cameras.

“They exonerate more law enforcement than they convict, and I want officers to wear body cameras because I want the American people to see what the ⁠officers saw when they took that action,” he said.

The Associated Press contributed to this report

text:
(NewsNation) — After NewsNation reported unaccompanied migrant minors were appearing in immigration court without legal representation, the Department of Health and Human services announced it reached a co-op agreement with a Texas law firm to provide counsel.

NewsNation learned that of the more than 1,800 migrant minors who arrive at the border unaccompanied by an adult, anywhere between 40% and 70% (depending on the week) were arriving in court without legal representation, despite an existing contract for a Washington D.C.-based law firm to do so.

The federal government was fully funding the deal, paying an estimated $20 million per month as part of a contract with the firm Acacia Center for Justice to represent the minors in court hearings.

On Friday, the Office of Refugee Resettlement told NewsNation exclusively it was partnering with Burke Law Group based in Houston to provide legal counsel through the rest of the year.

“In addition to representation during immigration proceedings and TVPRA requirements, the final recipient of the grant will also provide limited discharge-related legal continuity planning and referral support to assist children in connecting with appropriate post-discharge legal resources,” an ORR spokesperson told NewsNation.

The Acacia Center for Justice was asked to provide its basic billing information after its contract ended on July 31, which it declined to provide ORR, NewsNation learned.

“ORR is committed to ensuring every UAC has legal representation in immigration court, which is why ORR began using the U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants (USCRI) to provide legal representation to all UAC in ORR care,” John Fabbricatore, a senior adviser to HHS and ORR, told NewsNation.

Additionally, he stated the $150 million contract Burke Law was working on applying for does not mean they will receive the full amount as part of this agreement.

“There has been a lot of misinformation reported about the Burke Law Firm. They were not given a $150 million contract. They were working on applying for a grant to be able to help out with this effort. $150 million is the ceiling that the grant was funded for. This is not the amount being paid to Burke Law Firm. Burke Law Firm was applying for the opportunity to be used as a stop-gap and emergency partner to ensure that all UACs had legal representation,” Fabbricatore said.

“HHS and ORR are committed to ensuring that all UACs are represented in court and we have followed through with multiple lines of effort to ensure that mission is accomplished,” he also said.

Discrepancies in Acacia Center for Justice cases

Last week, Fabbricatore told NewsNation the agency began noticing discrepancies in the cases in which Acacia said it had represented migrant minors.

In some of those cases, those children were no longer in the United States, and in other cases, there were discrepancies in the age of the children receiving legal representation. He also said, in many cases, Acacia was declining to provide information that ORR had already provided and was asking for in return, raising more red flags.

“I think it’s important for the American taxpayer and for these children to make sure that with the money that we’re putting out, every child has a representative,” Fabbricatore said.

He added: “We need to really examine all of the records to determine if there was some fraud there. I don’t want to come forward and say there actually was, but that’s why it’s important to work together to ensure that the services we are paying for … are actually being provided.”

In a statement provided to NewsNation last week, Acacia accused the federal government of demanding confidential information it has no legal right to obtain. The law firm also says the federal government owes Acacia $65 million for legal services that have already been provided.

“The Trump administration is trying to sabotage this program by challenging paperwork as a pretext to strip away legal rights for thousands of undocumented children,” Acacia told NewsNation in a prepared statement. “This issue is not about paperwork or even nonpayment of the bills it owes.

“It’s about more than 20,000 vulnerable immigrant children who deserve to have someone in their corner and not be left alone without legal counsel to navigate our very complex immigration system.”

In its statement to NewsNation, the law firm says it provides legal representation to as many children as possible within the constraints of the funding provided by ORR.

The firm maintains the contract does not provide enough money for all the children it is contracted to represent to receive those services. It did not specifically address a question about whether it declined a bridge contract with ORR that would extend beyond Friday.

“We will do everything we can to protect vulnerable immigrant children and ensure they have the legal protection they deserve,” the firm’s statement said.

In response to Acacia’s claims about not being paid for services rendered, ORR told NewsNation in the United States, services are delivered and paid for with proof. A governmental contract is no exception.

“The government has every right to know which children in its custody are receiving the legal representation that the American taxpayer is paying for,” the agency said last week. “Demanding basic accountability is not unreasonable, it is a minimum standard.”

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement is moving to equip officers with body cameras in the next two months but the agency’s policy gives it broad control over what footage will be made public by specifying any releases must be in its “best interests.”

After years of delays, ICE said its field officers nationwide will have body-worn cameras by the end of September.

The rollout comes after recent fatal shootings by officers enforcing President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown have intensified pressure for accountability that the cameras could provide.

But the agency’s body-worn camera policy could mean taxpayers who are pitching in tens of millions of dollars to pay for the cameras may be kept in the dark about some high-profile confrontations, at least in their immediate aftermath.

The policy says ICE will promptly release video of shootings and other encounters in which its agents cause death or serious injury only after determining “it is in the best interests of the agency” to do so. That gives its director discretion to release recordings that reflect well on the agency’s image while working to keep others secret, experts on body camera policies said.

Such selective releases are routine in some law enforcement agencies but usually not so clearly contemplated in policy, according to professor Christopher Schneider of Brandon University in Canada, a co-author of the new book “Police Body-Worn Cameras: Media and the New Discourse of Police Reform.”

“In some ways, ICE is saying the quiet part out loud,” he said. “Body-worn cameras are being used as contemporary image-work tools to present the police to the public in the most favorable way possible.”

Body camera policy allows withholding some video

The policy requires officers to activate cameras during routine enforcement activities, including while making arrests, executing search warrants and responding to emergencies.

After shootings or other serious confrontations, a committee that includes top ICE officials and lawyers will review footage and recommend whether to release it promptly, according to the body camera policy issued in February 2025.

If the answer is yes, the recording could be released within 72 hours. But if the ICE director finds that “specific and compelling circumstances” justify withholding the video, they have the authority to block or indefinitely delay the release, the policy says.

The policy does not elaborate on such circumstances, and ICE did not respond to a question from The Associated Press about how it would make such decisions.

Practices vary widely in the U.S. In Chicago, a police watchdog agency routinely releases body camera video of shootings and other serious use-of-force incidents within 60 days. In Philadelphia, the police department very rarely uses its discretion to release video of specific incidents and has no policy for when to do so.

Even when footage is released, ICE’s policy will require the redaction of all officers’ identifying features such as their faces, names and badge numbers to preserve their privacy.

Schneider, who has studied body cameras since their use began spreading a decade ago, said he does not expect ICE to release footage of fatal shootings like those last month in Houston and Maine.

He noted ICE’s sister agency, Customs and Border Protection, has not released footage of the January shooting of Alex Pretti in Minneapolis even though it was captured on agents’ cameras. CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott told lawmakers in February that the video and other materials were under investigation and would be made public “when it’s appropriate.”

ICE says all officers will have cameras by end of September

ICE spent $30.9 million in July to purchase body camera equipment from Axon, the Arizona-based company that also manufactures Tasers, federal spending records show.

The spending began one day after the fatal shooting of a 25-year-old motorist in Maine by an ICE officer with a history of violent behavior. Days earlier, another ICE officer shot and killed a homebuilder in Houston who was driving to work.

Neither shooting was recorded with body cameras. That news angered members of Congress, who had given ICE $20 million to purchase body cameras in a bill passed to end a partial government shutdown on April 30.

ICE said body cameras have been sent to more than half its field officers and the rest will receive them by the end of September. That timeline pushes back estimates from earlier public statements. Maine Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who backed funding for cameras, said last month that the agency informed her they would be deployed by the end of August. ICE had said earlier that they would be issued by mid-September.

ICE officers working in the Houston area, where the agency sent more than 800 cameras, are among those who have started training, according to U.S. Rep. Henry Cuellar, a Texas Democrat and member of the House Appropriations Committee.

At least one member of every arrest team will be required to have a camera, the agency said.

“I think the American people need to see what that officer sees and hears,” White House border czar Tom Homan said July 19 on CBS News’ “Face the Nation.” “And if you look at the data, body cameras actually exonerate agents more than they, you know, provide evidence of wrongdoing.”

Schneider said he expects ICE to release recordings that promote the agency’s mass deportation program by portraying officers as brave and immigrants as dangerous criminals.

“Much of what law enforcement does is convince the public that we need them and feel safe and they do all this good stuff for us,” he said. “The more bad stuff the public sees, the more angry the public gets. And this causes problems for the police brand.”

ICE has taken years to adopt body cameras

ICE began testing body cameras in 2021 during President Joe Biden’s administration and distributed 1,400 devices three years later, saying use would expand as funding became available.

After returning to office in 2025, President Donald Trump rescinded a Biden order that required federal law enforcement agencies to use body cameras.

ICE did not buy body cameras even after it received a historic $75 billion infusion in Trump’s signature policy bill in 2025 and began hiring thousands of new officers. The two July purchases from Axon were made through an existing government contract that began in 2023, records show.

“This is not hard to deploy, but they’ve slow-rolled it,” said Jason Houser, who was ICE chief of staff under Biden and helped implement the agency’s pilot program.

Houser said the Trump administration should have equipped officers with body cameras when it expanded mass arrests and traffic stops. Doing so only after several shootings and pressure from Congress “is clearly a political response” that will not make officers or the public safer, he said.

“This doesn’t fix the problem of putting officers in a place where they’re not trained or equipped to carry out the style of operations that the administration is asking them to do,” he said.

text:
The death of a New Jersey father at Delaney Hall immigration detention center this week has reignited long-held frustration about federal agencies’ alleged mistreatment of detainees and their handling of the dead and dying in custody.

Many of the details surrounding the death of 39-year-old Edwin Jovanny Lopez-Cornejo remain unclear almost a week after he died on Saturday. According to a statement from Immigration and Customs Enforcement — which misstated his age, according to family members — “a 41-year-old illegal alien from El Salvador who was detained at Delaney Hall Detention Facility, was pronounced deceased Aug. 1 by medical personnel at University Hospital in Newark, New Jersey.”

Family members, alongside a host of New Jersey lawmakers and immigration advocates, characterize the story differently: Lopez-Cornejo, the father of a 12-year-old girl, called his mom to report that he wasn’t feeling well, and claimed that Delaney Hall staff members weren’t giving him his medication.

“He couldn’t feel half of his face or right hand,” said Jorge Torres, a member of the National Day Laborer Organizing Network, who spoke alongside Lopez-Cornejo’s mother, Maria, at the press conference Tuesday. “Edwin, like countless other people detained at Delaney Hall and other ICE prisoners across the country, had not received his proper medication regime, and for his diabetes, high blood pressure, and seizures.”

Family members and local lawmakers argue that Lopez-Cornejo was the victim not only of what his mother called “medical negligence,” but a wider alleged plot by the Department of Homeland Security to release the dead and dying to area hospitals, and avoid adding their names to the growing list of deaths at federal facilities. ICE reports 55 deaths at detention centers nationally since January 2025 — but lawmakers and immigration experts argue that the number could be much higher, given the opaque and ever-changing nature of DHS agencies’ reporting policies.

That confusion was laid bare after Lopez-Cornejo’s death: Lawmakers say he was one of three people to die at Delaney Hall in less than a year, including 41-year-old Jean Wilson Brutus, who died at the facility in December on the same day of his intake examination. Rep. Rob Menendez said he learned of a third death at the facility this week during an unannounced oversight visit; but said ICE didn’t count the death in its mandatory report to Congress because the person was released and technically declared dead at a local hospital.

“I have often found that ICE’s accounting of many incidents are not accurate,” Menendez said Monday during a press call. “My conversations with both advocates and detained individuals is that they are increasing the number of people being moved into Delaney Hall, and increasing the number of people being moved out. So there is an immense amount of transition at the facility, and I raise the question with the number of individuals there … that has to create a challenging environment to administer healthcare properly.”

On Thursday, a delegation of House Democrats in Jersey sent a public letter to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin detailing “disturbing allegations” of “inadequate care for the medically vulnerable.” And they criticized a directive reportedly issued this week by ICE acting Director David Venturella to rescind a policy requiring the agency to notify the public when a detainee dies within 30 days of their release from custody. (A DHS official confirmed the change with The Washington Post, saying it was “common sense” that ICE should not be responsible for deaths happening outside facilities.)

“That policy existed for a reason: our government’s responsibility does not end at the detention center gate,” reads the letter, signed by nine New Jersey Democrats including its sponsor, Rep. Analilia Mejia. “Eliminating that transparency does not change the facts, but can serve to hide information from the American public purposefully.”

In a statement to MS NOW, a DHS spokesperson disputed the claims about Lopez-Cornejo’s mistreatment and inadequate medical care at ICE facilities. The statement read, in part:

“ICE is committed to ensuring that all those in custody reside in safe, secure and humane environments. Comprehensive medical care is provided from the moment individuals arrive and throughout their stay. … At no time during detention is a detained noncitizen denied emergency care.”

Recommended

Deaths at immigration detention centers have increased rapidly under Trump, experts say.

“The mortality rate of deaths in ICE custody is at its highest level in over a decade and has more than doubled since Trump’s second term began. The rate is nearly four times that of the Biden administration, and more than two and a half times as high as that of the first Trump administration,” reads a June 2026 report by the Human Rights Watch.

A recent analysis by Physicians for Human Rights looked at 39 reported deaths under ICE and found that in all cases, “the government did not publicly provide sufficient information about the circumstances of death or about the medical care provided in detention to support a definitive clinical assessment.”

Scrutiny is mounting this week over how the federal government documents the dead. The Pentagon recently altered requirements for how military deaths in the Iran war are recorded, lowering the number of casualties reported on its website from the Middle East conflict.

Lopez-Cornejo’s death, and that of the person who Menendez says died at Delaney Hall in July, have not been added to ICE’s detainee death database as of this week. It’s unclear how their deaths might be treated based on ICE’s policies.

Now, Lopez-Cornejo’s family is demanding an independent investigation into his death from New Jersey’s attorney general, access to his medical records and the release of all detainees at the facility. They also called on Gov. Mikie Sherrill to investigate the conditions at Delaney Hall.

“Edwin should still be alive. His death demands more than condolences. It demands justice. No one, no one should lose their life in detention because of neglect, indifference, or a system that fails to protect basic human dignity,” Torres said.

MS NOW reporter Laura Haefeli contributed to this report.

title: During Operation Metro Surge, ICE arrested dozens of immigrant crime victims
description:

The arrest of immigrant crime victims undercuts a public safety tool created by Congress to combat crime and strengthen relationships between immigrants and law enforcement agencies.

In 2012, when the Violence Against Women Act was up for renewal, GOP members of Congress soured on the legislation in part because of its protections for immigrant crime victims.
text:
Years ago, Rosa watched from inside the car as men robbed her husband at gunpoint, shortly after they’d arrived in Minnesota from Guatemala.

The couple had a pending asylum case, but once they reported the crime to the police, they were eligible for a U visa, which provides a path to legal permanent residency for victims of and witnesses to serious crimes — and, in some cases, their immediate family members. At her request, the Reformer is using Rosa’s first name to protect her from government retribution.

Rosa is among dozens of people who were detained by immigration authorities during Operation Metro Surge in Minnesota, despite having permission to live and work in the United States because they were victims of a crime and reported it to the police.

One man survived a shooting in 2019 that took him out of work for six months and left him permanently disabled. Another was stabbed in the leg during a 2016 robbery in Minneapolis. Others survived human trafficking, felony assaults and armed robberies.

In one case, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents broke down a family’s front door and arrested all three people inside — without a warrant, according to the lawsuit.

The Reformer analyzed more than 1,100 habeas corpus petitions — federal lawsuits challenging a person’s detention — filed in Minnesota between December and mid-March and identified at least 75 people who were detained by immigration agencies despite having been granted work permits and deportation protections allowed to crime victims.

That number is likely an undercount. Many immigrants did not have access to attorneys for long stretches, couldn’t afford legal fees, or were shipped out of state before their lawyers could file the lawsuit in Minnesota.

In May, a federal judge ordered ICE to revert to its previous policy of not arresting crime victims, temporarily, while a lawsuit works its way through the courts.

Many of the crime victims who filed lawsuits over their detention won and returned to their families in Minnesota, and are now fighting the deportation proceedings initiated by their arrest.

President Donald Trump has remade the immigration court system to support his mass deportation campaign, however, so even people who have been issued work permits and deportation protections face an uphill battle to stay in the U.S.

ICE did not respond to the Reformer’s emailed questions for this story.

The arrest of immigrant crime victims undercuts a public safety tool created by Congress to combat crime and strengthen relationships between immigrants and law enforcement agencies. The shift in policy, however, fulfills a longstanding Republican goal to roll back the protections provided to immigrants under the program.

When Congress formalized the U visa program as part of a renewal of the Violence Against Women Act of 2000, members of both political parties agreed on the need for a law protecting undocumented victims of crimes. The U visa is an expanded version of the T visa, which offers protections for undocumented victims of human trafficking.

Congress created the U visa “out of recognition that victims without legal status may otherwise be reluctant to help in the investigation or prosecution of criminal activity,” according to Department of Homeland Security guidance.

Public safety and policing experts say the U visa program helps local police officers build trust with undocumented communities by assuring crime victims that they won’t be deported for seeking help from the police — the same logic that underlies many local police departments’ separation from immigration authorities.

A bona fide determination

Rosa and her family applied for a U visa in 2023, which required a certification document from local police confirming that Rosa’s husband had reported the robbery and cooperated with investigators.

But there was one major issue: Congress had capped the number of U visas issued per year at 10,000. The year Rosa’s family submitted their application, the backlog of applications surpassed 344,000, or a 34-year waitlist.

In 2021, the administration of President Joe Biden found a way to help people waiting for their visas. U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services would review the pending applications — running criminal background checks and checking law enforcement certifications — and issue a “bona fide determination” to immigrants whose applications met the U visa criteria, but for whom there were no available visas.

Two years after Rosa and her husband applied for the visa, and one month into President Donald Trump’s second term, they received a letter in the mail from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

“The evidence demonstrates that … they warrant a favorable exercise of discretion to receive employment authorization and deferred action,” the letter read, meaning work permits and protection from deportation while they waited for the full visa, which would provide a path to permanent residency. In the meantime, they needed to stay in the country, not commit any crimes and attend regular check-ins with ICE.

Rosa walked into the Whipple Federal Building, the headquarters of ICE in Minnesota, on Jan. 23 with her husband, their 6-year-old daughter and the paperwork they needed for a routine check-in. Friends had warned Rosa not to go to the meeting because many people never returned, but Rosa’s husband reassured her: “We have paperwork,” she remembers him saying.

After sitting in a waiting room for eight hours, Rosa said, three agents entered. They placed handcuffs on her husband, informed the family they would be separated, and whisked her husband out the door.

Then, the agents ushered Rosa and her daughter in and out of hallways and holding cells, on and off airplanes. They spent the night on the floor of a room. Rosa had no idea where they were. Her daughter kept asking where her dad was. Neither of them could stop crying.

Operation Metro Surge and beyond

Ten days after Trump assumed the presidency for the second time, the acting director of ICE issued a memo to all agency employees, reversing decades of policies that instructed agents not to detain immigrants with pending U visas.

Shortly after, immigration authorities began arresting people around the country who had been granted work permits and deportation protections under the program. The Trump administration has similarly rolled back protections for refugees, asylum seekers and other categories of immigrants.

By the time ICE agents swarmed Minnesota this winter, the agency was treating people with pending U visas as fair game for deportation.

Marcos Lopez Garcia arrived in Minnesota from his rural Mexican town as a teenager. He dropped out of school at 13 to help with his family’s farm, and crossed the U.S. border in search of better job opportunities. He met his wife, also a teenager at the time, at their job cleaning Minneapolis hotel rooms. They settled in Bloomington and had four children, all citizens, the oldest now in her mid-20s. Lopez Garcia worked his way into a management position at a commercial cleaning company.

At one of his cleaning jobs, a co-worker repeatedly came onto him, asking him to leave his family for her. Each time he refused, she grew angrier, until she threatened to report him and his wife to immigration authorities. In June 2022, she showed up at his home uninvited.

He called the police to report the crimes. The Bloomington Police Department certified on his U visa application that he had been a victim of blackmail and extortion and that he was cooperative.

ICE arrested him on his way to work on Jan. 26, shipped him to Texas and held him for two weeks before his lawyer won his release.

Kevin Ramirez Mancia hitchhiked from Honduras to Minnesota with his father when he was 13. They settled in Willmar, a city of 20,000 people, 100 miles west of the Twin Cities.

Ramirez Mancia attended Willmar Senior High School while his father worked in a nearby egg factory. In November of his sophomore year, he was at his desk singing a song and waving his hands to the music. Another classmate thought Ramirez Mancia was making signs at him, and flipped him off. Ramirez Mancia kept singing.

The classmate took a knife out of his backpack and walked toward Ramirez Mancia, the knife pointing toward his neck.

“I thought he was going to stab me,” Ramirez Mancia said.

He got the attention of the teacher, who confiscated the knife and called the principal, who notified the police. Ramirez Mancia told the officer what happened, and that evening, police arrested the student who had threatened Ramirez Mancia, according to the incident report.

In 2023, Ramirez Mancia applied for a U visa based on his status as a victim of second-degree assault and threats of violence, and received his work permit and deferred action — protection from deportation.

On April 4, police pulled over Ramirez Mancia, now 20, and arrested him on suspicion of driving under the influence of cannabis and possessing a pistol without a permit, resulting in three misdemeanor charges. As he was waiting for his release paperwork, an ICE officer approached and informed him he was being taken into immigration custody.

He spent exactly four months in Freeborn County Jail, which holds immigrants on behalf of ICE. On Tuesday, a judge ordered his release; he will remain free while he appeals his deportation order.

A politicized program

Republican politicians have long criticized the U visa program, arguing that the list of qualifying crimes — blackmail, domestic violence, obstruction of justice and felonious assault among them — is too broad. In 2012, when the Violence Against Women Act was up for renewal, GOP members of Congress soured on the legislation in part because of its protections for immigrant crime victims.

“(Violence Against Women Act) is meant to protect victims of violence. It shouldn’t be an avenue to expand immigration law or to give additional benefits to people here unlawfully,” Sen. Chuck Grassley, an Iowa Republican, said in a 2012 Judiciary Committee hearing before Congress ultimately renewed the law without major changes to the U visa provisions.

Project 2025, the roadmap for President Donald Trump’s second term, called for the total elimination of U and T visas.

“Victimization should not be a basis for an immigration benefit…. Pending elimination of the T and U visas, the Secretary should significantly restrict eligibility for each visa to prevent fraud,” the document reads.

Richard Hodsdon, general counsel for the Minnesota Sheriffs’ Association and a former prosecutor, said U visas “certainly can support public safety from a victim perspective.”

They can also be used for “manipulation and abuse,” he added.

Defense attorneys, Hodsdon said, sometimes asked for U visas for their clients as part of a plea negotiation, seeking compensation for flipping on co-conspirators.

A handful of high-profile fraud cases have bolstered Republicans’ argument. In 2023, the U.S. Department of Justice announced charges against multiple men accused of staging armed robberies at convenience stores to create pathways for U visas for the “victims.” The ringleaders in that case pleaded guilty, and in March, the feds charged 11 additional people for their participation in the plot.

And in July 2025, the DOJ charged five Louisiana men in an alleged scheme to falsify police reports for U visa applications.

“(Those cases) are symptomatic of a bigger problem, which is that desperate people do desperate things, and if we had an immigration system that worked in an effective and efficient way, you wouldn’t have desperate people doing desperate things,” said Rekha Sharma-Crawford, a Kansas City-based attorney who serves on the executive committee of the American Immigration Lawyers Association.

In limbo

A coalition of California-based immigrants and activist organizations sued ICE in October over its treatment of people with pending U and T — trafficking — visas.

“ICE now routinely detains and deports people who have valid grants of deferred action from USCIS in connection with pending U or T visa petitions,” according to the lawsuit.

The Trump administration has found other ways to slow down the process of obtaining the visas or associated work permits: delaying confirmation of receipt of applications, prolonging processing times and nitpicking applications, according to the lawsuit and interviews with immigration attorneys.

“USCIS is (starting) with the idea that we are going to deny the application, and then if they can overcome that and somehow convince you, then maybe we will think it over. That’s the attitude of the agency right now,” Sharma-Crawford said.

In May, a federal judge temporarily voided the 2025 ICE memo that permitted agents to detain crime victims with pending U and T visas. Since then, the arrest of such people has slowed, Sharma-Crawford said.

“But that doesn’t mean that they won’t try and either disregard a court order or appeal it,” she added.

For many families, the damage is already done.

After their series of flights and holding cells, Rosa and her 6-year-old daughter arrived at the processing center of the South Texas Family Detention Center in Dilley. They spent 26 days in detention before a judge ordered their release.

Every member of her family is still terrified. They’ve relied on support from staff at her daughter’s school to make ends meet. Her daughter complains of her chest hurting — possibly from anxiety, Rosa said — and can’t sleep.

“My daughter still hasn’t recovered from this,” Rosa said, her voice shaking. She hasn’t recovered, either.

text:
WASHINGTON — As the Trump administration expands immigration enforcement and accelerates deportation proceedings, Democratic lawmakers are pushing legislation that would establish a federal right to legal representation for people facing deportation who cannot afford an attorney.

Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif., introduced the Fairness to Freedom Act of 2026 on Thursday, legislation that would require the federal government to provide legal representation in immigration proceedings, including deportation cases, bond hearings and expedited removal proceedings. The legislation comes as advocates warn that hundreds of thousands of immigrants are navigating a complex legal system without attorneys while facing detention, family separation and removal from the United States.

Unlike people charged in criminal court, immigrants facing removal proceedings generally do not have a right to a government-funded attorney because immigration proceedings are civil rather than criminal. People may hire attorneys, but those unable to afford counsel can be required to represent themselves even when deportation is at stake.

“President Trump’s cruel immigration agenda has caused unimaginable, long-lasting harm in our communities, leading to unlawful deportations that have torn thousands of families apart,” Schiff said. “Having access to legal counsel during immigration proceedings is essential to fair outcomes, yet beyond the reach of many.”

“Our nation has been shaped for the better by the extraordinary contributions of immigrants, and I’m leading this bill to ensure that families have a fighting chance to present their cases and achieve fair results in the courts,” Schiff added.

The legislation is backed by the Fairness to Freedom campaign, co-led by the Vera Institute of Justice and the National Partnership for New Americans.

According to Vera, legal representation can dramatically affect the outcome of immigration proceedings. A recent Vera study found that people facing deportation who had legal representation were 4.7 times more likely to obtain relief than people without attorneys.

Yet representation has become increasingly difficult to obtain. Research cited by Schiff’s office found that only about 34% of people whose immigration court cases were completed so far in fiscal year 2026 had attorneys, the lowest representation rate since 2010.

The disparities in outcomes are substantial.

From fiscal years 2016 through 2025, people facing deportation without attorneys were ordered removed in 78% of completed cases, compared with 27% of those represented by attorneys, according to research cited by Schiff’s office. As of June, more than half of the more than 3.1 million pending removal cases in immigration court — at least 1.6 million cases — involved people without representation.

Dr. Austin Kocher, president of Relevant Research, said the data demonstrate the importance of counsel in a system where the consequences can include permanent separation from family and removal from the country.

“After years of studying the immigration courts, one thing is absolutely clear in the data: access to legal representation is easily one of the most important factors in whether immigrants facing deportation get a fair hearing,” Kocher said. “Representation rates are at their lowest point since 2010. Even many children are forced to sit in court alone without an attorney.”

The Fairness to Freedom Act would require the federal government to establish a right to counsel for people who cannot afford representation in a broad range of immigration matters.

The legislation would cover people facing deportation and bond hearings as well as certain state court proceedings and matters before U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, including special immigrant juvenile status, U visas and Temporary Protected Status applications. It would also guarantee representation for people subjected to expedited removal at the border.

The bill calls for early, continuous, full-scope and high-quality representation and would amend the Immigration and Nationality Act to create an Office of Immigration Representation. It would also coordinate federal representation with existing state and locally funded deportation defense programs.

Vera reported that more than 80 state and local jurisdictions across 28 states have created or funded immigration legal representation programs during the past decade. State and local investment in deportation defense has nearly doubled since 2025, increasing from approximately $260 million to more than $500 million nationwide.

The 2026 legislation would also remove what advocates describe as an administrative obstacle to obtaining counsel by eliminating the wet-signature requirement on Department of Homeland Security forms.

Rep. Norma Torres, D-Calif., who has led the legislation in the House, said the ability to defend against deportation should not depend on financial resources.

“For years, I have proudly led the Fairness to Freedom Act in the House because I believe due process should never depend on a person’s ability to afford an attorney,” Torres said. “Today, as the Trump Administration escalates attacks on immigrant communities and undermines fundamental legal protections, that mission has never been more urgent.”

“Together, we are making it clear that no one should face detention or deportation alone simply because they cannot afford legal representation,” Torres added. “Justice should not be reserved for those who can pay for it.”

Sens. Cory Booker, D-N.J.; Alex Padilla, D-Calif.; Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y.; Jeff Merkley, D-Ore.; Ron Wyden, D-Ore.; and Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., are Senate co-sponsors. Torres is leading the legislation in the House with Reps. Grace Meng, D-N.Y.; Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash.; and Robert Garcia, D-Calif.

Booker said the lack of representation leaves immigrants attempting to navigate complicated proceedings while facing potentially life-altering consequences.

“Immigrants are being pushed through complex legal proceedings without legal representation, forced to navigate a confusing system alone as they fight for their freedom, their futures, and, for many, the chance to keep their families together,” Booker said. “This legislation helps ensure that no one has to face that system alone by providing the legal support they need to receive a fair hearing.”

Gillibrand similarly framed the legislation as a matter of due process.

“No one should be deprived of the fundamental right to due process, basic fairness, and human dignity in our immigration system,” Gillibrand said. “It’s time to make commonsense reforms.”

“The Fairness to Freedom Act would ensure every person subject to immigration proceedings is guaranteed legal representation, leading to a more equitable and transparent system that gives immigrants a fair chance,” Gillibrand added.

Padilla said financial circumstances should not determine whether someone has an attorney while navigating the immigration system.

“Everyone deserves access to legal representation during the immigration process, and no one should be denied legal counsel because of their inability to pay,” Padilla said. “As the Trump Administration continues its assault on due process and targets vulnerable communities, we must ensure immigrant communities understand their rights and have access to strong legal counsel.”

“Our bill would help ensure that no one is forced to navigate our complex immigration system alone, protecting the dignity and fundamental fairness at the heart of our justice system,” Padilla added.

Garcia contrasted the protections available in criminal court with those afforded to immigrants facing removal.

“People facing criminal charges in this country have the right to a lawyer, but immigrants facing deportation often do not,” Garcia said. “As ICE raids under the Trump Administration threaten people’s constitutional rights, guaranteeing access to legal counsel is more important than ever. I’m proud to support this bill to protect due process.”

The legislation comes amid intensified federal immigration enforcement and growing concern among advocates about whether immigrants can meaningfully exercise their legal rights without attorneys.

Vera pointed to increased immigration enforcement, large-scale immigration court hearings and expanded detention, along with the loss of legal status for hundreds of thousands of Temporary Protected Status holders and threats to legal representation for immigrant children, as factors increasing the urgency of universal representation.

Shayna Kessler, director of Vera’s Advancing Universal Representation initiative and co-leader of the Fairness to Freedom campaign, said access to counsel is fundamental to meaningful due process.

“The Fairness to Freedom Act is an urgently needed piece of legislation to establish a right to federally funded legal representation for anyone facing deportation,” Kessler said.

“This is about due process, keeping families together, protecting vulnerable children, and ensuring people have their fair day in court at a time when the Trump administration has trampled those rights and values,” Kessler added. “No one should be denied the opportunity to defend their freedom simply because they cannot afford an attorney.”

Nicole Melaku, executive director of the National Partnership for New Americans and co-leader of the Fairness to Freedom campaign, said legal representation has become increasingly important as federal immigration enforcement expands.

“Our families and communities are under attack by the federal government, and it’s time we give adults and children facing deportation the most effective support they need: a lawyer by their side,” Melaku said.

“Since day one of his second term, President Trump has widened the dragnet of who is at risk, greased the wheels of the deportation pipeline, and deepened the due process crisis in our immigration courts,” Melaku added. “In a system that grows more punitive by the day, access to a lawyer is one of the strongest shields against wrongful detention, family separation, and deportation.”

The legislation faces significant political obstacles in a Republican-controlled Congress. But supporters argue the widening disparity between the government’s power to arrest, detain and deport immigrants and the ability of those immigrants to obtain legal representation makes congressional action increasingly urgent.
