title: Project 2025: As midterms near, Trump's window for action might be closing
description:
But the clock is ticking on the administration’s ability to complete much more of the Project 2025 agenda.
“Every day that President Trump rolls out another Project 2025 item, it’s really an endorsement of our work,” he said.
Project 2025 also proposed defunding Planned Parenthood, which faced a one-year ban on funding from Medicaid but has seen that funding restored since July 5.
Another goal of Project 2025 was for the Department of Education to be shut down.
But the Trump administration has worked around congressional approval to move forward on other Project 2025 items.
text:
During his 2024 campaign for president, Donald Trump famously disavowed Project 2025, a conservative blueprint for governing produced by the Heritage Foundation. “I don’t know anything about it, I don’t want to know anything about it,” he said, dismissing its agenda as “seriously extreme.”

Once back in office, however, President Trump pursued many of the proposals in Project 2025, as he and his administration sought to enact sweeping change over the federal government and broad swaths of American life.

To date, more than half of Project 2025’s policy recommendations have been enacted, according to a Heritage fundraising email from June 23, as well as several organizations tracking the administration’s actions. Many of those moves happened in the first few months of his second term: Mr. Trump signed a flurry of executive orders on everything from immigration to climate change, slashed staff at some federal agencies and all but eliminated others, and has refused to spend some money appropriated by Congress.

But the clock is ticking on the administration’s ability to complete much more of the Project 2025 agenda. If the fall midterm elections bring Democratic control of one or both chambers of Congress, it could slow or challenge the rest of Mr. Trump’s priorities.

Some of those involved with or supportive of Project 2025 say they’re pleased with what the administration has accomplished so far, while wondering if even more could have been achieved.

Most of the document’s goals were not new or exclusive to Heritage, which for decades has authored policy guides for GOP administrations; many have long been part of the conservative wish-list. A senior fellow at the Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation and Institute says that Mr. Trump’s denunciation of the document on the campaign trail might have given it a notoriety beyond a “typical think tank pre-election policy book” that made it harder for the administration to execute some of its ideas.

The architects ultimately got some of what they wanted, says Tevi Troy, a presidential historian and former senior White House aide under President George W. Bush. But he adds, “I think the question within the leadership at Heritage has got to be, ‘What would it have been if this thing didn’t blow up and Trump didn’t denounce it?’”

A fast start

One of the things Project 2025’s architects understood was the need for speed.

James Goodwin, policy director for the Center for Progressive Reform, which has been tracking proposals completed by executive action, says that, in its early days, the administration produced the equivalent of one policy accomplishment per day.

Mr. Goodwin, whose organization calls Project 2025 a guide to weaken American democracy, says that the Trump administration has moved quickly in part by ignoring norms.

“It just doesn’t care about, is unconcerned about being perceived as cruel or operating in bad faith,” he says.

Paul Dans, one of the architects of Project 2025 and the former director of the 2025 Presidential Transition Project at Heritage, told NPR that watching Mr. Trump sign a flurry of executive orders based on the blueprint’s recommendations was momentous.

“Every day that President Trump rolls out another Project 2025 item, it’s really an endorsement of our work,” he said. A Heritage Foundation spokesperson tells the Monitor in a statement that the organization is “proud to continue developing and advancing common-sense policy solutions that improve the lives of Americans.”

Mandy Gunasekara, a lawyer who was chief of staff at the Environmental Protection Agency during Mr. Trump’s first term, penned Project 2025’s section on the EPA. In an interview with the Monitor, she said it was important that policies be moved forward in the first 100 days.

“Getting your major initiatives advanced in the first 100 days is key to their success,” says Ms. Gunasekara. “And that’s a lesson that we learned the hard way during the first Trump administration, and why things like Project 2025 ... had game plans, not just of policy goals, but staff training and personnel recommendations ready to go on Day 1.”

A notable success, she says, was the repeal of the 2009 Endangerment Finding. That was a scientific determination that deemed six major greenhouse gases (including carbon dioxide and methane) to be a threat to public health, giving the EPA power to regulate greenhouse gas emissions. Democratic officials such as California Gov. Gavin Newsom and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York criticized the reversal, saying the administration was putting the interests of fossil-fuel industries ahead of the American people.

“Trump is making a radical move that will send shockwaves across the economy – uncertainty for manufacturers, states, regulators everywhere. And it flies in the face, of course, of basic science,” Mr. Schumer said on the Senate floor in February, calling the move “a corrupt giveaway to Big Oil, plain and simple.”

David R. Burton, a senior research fellow at Advancing American Freedom, a conservative advocacy and policy organization, wrote recommendations in Project 2025 regarding the Securities and Exchange Commission and other financial regulators. That section suggested, for example, the reduction of “regulatory impediments” on entrepreneurs that affect their capital gains. He suggests that there is still work to be done.

Some predict the administration will be motivated to try to get as much done as possible in the remaining months before the fall midterms. Mr. Trump and Republicans are facing significant headwinds going into the elections, with public opinion on the president’s overall job performance at or near 60% disapproval.

“There definitely is going to be a push before this election in the event that one or both of the houses flip,” says Ms. Gunasekara.

Yet, if the administration makes a push to enact more items from the Project 2025 wish list, one expert says, it could actually make the midterms even more challenging for the GOP.

“I find that the more that [a] president achieves their policy goals in Congress, the worse they do in the subsequent midterm elections, because when you move the ball visibly in one ideological direction, public opinion tends to move in the other direction,” says Matt Grossmann, the director of the Institute for Public Policy and Social Research at Michigan State University.

Unfinished business

Many policies in Project 2025 have not been put in place.

On the topic of abortion, the policy blueprint calls for nationwide restrictions. Though 13 states now have complete abortion bans, and others have imposed strict limitations, there are no nationwide restrictions. Project 2025 also proposed defunding Planned Parenthood, which faced a one-year ban on funding from Medicaid but has seen that funding restored since July 5.

Another goal of Project 2025 was for the Department of Education to be shut down. Heritage has long argued that educational choices should be made by states and parents, not the federal government.

Last March, President Trump cut nearly half of the department’s staff and ordered its closure through executive action. But shuttering a federal agency requires congressional approval. In mid-July, the House Education and Workforce Committee advanced a 10-bill package that would dismantle the Education Department and allocate some of its mandate to other federal agencies. Congress has yet to act on it.

On immigration, Project 2025 proposals to mandate a nationwide E-Verify system for all private employers, and for the repeal of Temporary Protected Status as a program, are also waiting on congressional action.

But the Trump administration has worked around congressional approval to move forward on other Project 2025 items.

Upon taking office, President Trump signed executive orders to end diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives; to enforce a transgender military ban; to increase White House oversight in agencies such as the Justice Department; to reclassify many federal workers to be subject to executive branch supervision instead of being apolitical appointees; to ramp up deportations of unauthorized immigrants; and to close the country’s southern border.

More broadly, Mr. Trump and his administration have pursued another goal of Project 2025: expanding presidential authority over the executive branch.

Mr. Trump was handed a victory by the U.S. Supreme Court in June in Trump v. Slaughter. Rebecca Slaughter, a commissioner with the Federal Trade Commission, had challenged Mr. Trump’s decision to fire her. The court’s decision allows a president to fire heads of agencies that were created by Congress to be independent of the White House.

The Slaughter ruling will stand after Mr. Trump leaves office. However, policies enacted through executive orders rather than legislation passed by Congress might not last. That pattern has gone on for 35 years, says William Yeatman, director of the George Washington University’s Regulatory Studies Center.

“Anything one president can do, another president can undo,” says Mr. Yeatman.

Over 100 Maine Medical Center nurses and supporters rallied in Portland today, demanding the release of a colleague arrested by ICE last week.

According to the nurses union, registered nurse Debora Kapisha was arrested by ICE on July 30 at Boston's Logan Airport.

The union said Kapisha, originally from Zambia, is seeking asylum and has legal work authorization.

Nurse and union co-president Kelli Brennan said the arrest undercuts the Trump administration's own justification for its mass deportation agenda.

"This is not about safety. This is not about border security," Brennan said. "It is about stripping our friends and neighbors of their dignity, their safety, and any ability they have to comfortably live their lives."

And fellow nurse Abbey Nelson said Kapisha's absence is affecting coworkers and patients.

"Not only is it heartbreaking to see someone who has given so much to others be taken away, but it's angering and it's just sickening," she said. "She's a trusted colleague, a compassionate caregiver, and a person whose work has made a profound difference in the lives of countless patients."

Other speakers called on MaineHealth to support Kapisha in securing permanent legal status in the U.S.

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said in an email Wednesday that Kapisha had overstayed a visa.

MaineHealth said in a statement Wednesday that all employees are vetted to ensure they have legal authorization to live and work in the U.S.

"We have also reached out to our congressional delegation to see if they can provide any further information about this care team member’s status," said Britt Crewse, president of MaineHealth’s Southern Region, in the statement. "Needless to say, we are concerned, especially given that this individual appears to have been living and working here legally."

text:
An Argentine woman living in South Philadelphia was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement at Philadelphia International Airport while awaiting an asylum interview, according to her attorney and family.

Iliana Lick, 30, came to the United States from Argentina in 2023 on a tourist visa that was later extended. Her attorney said she was waiting for an asylum interview with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services when she was arrested on July 11.

Lick's boyfriend, Steven Mechiorre, said he drove her to Philadelphia International Airport that morning. After returning home, he received a phone call from Lick.

"I pick it up and it's Iliana crying, saying ICE arrested me," Mechiorre said.

"It hit me like a ton of bricks. I was devastated at that moment because I knew that everything had changed at this point," he said.

According to Mechiorre, Lick has since been transferred through several detention centers in Pennsylvania, Louisiana and Texas. She is now being held in New Mexico while awaiting an immigration court hearing that has been postponed several times.

The uncertainty has also weighed heavily on her family in Argentina.

"The feeling of uncertainty has been awful because you don't know what's going to happen or how this will all end," her father, Luis Lick, said.

Lick's immigration attorney, Ana Ferreira, said the arrest came as a surprise.

"It is shocking. I've been doing this for 11 years and we never encountered anything like this before," Ferreira said.

Ferreira said people in circumstances similar to Lick's had previously been able to travel domestically without incident but that she has recently seen more arrests like this.

According to Ferreira, Lick "was never even one day unlawfully" in the United States.

"She was doing everything that she could possibly be doing to try to remain in the U.S. lawfully," Ferreira said.

Lick's father described his daughter as a law-abiding person who has never had legal problems in Argentina or the United States.

He said he hopes her character and good behavior will help resolve the case so she can continue pursuing her dreams.

text:
On Aug. 5, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia confirmed that its prior order staying the termination of Haiti’s Temporary Protected Status (TPS) designation is no longer in effect following action by the U.S. Supreme Court and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit. As a result, the court-ordered injunction that had temporarily prevented the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) from implementing its termination of Haiti TPS has been lifted. TPS beneficiaries can no longer rely on the District Court’s stay as a basis for continued protection from the termination.

However, the underlying lawsuit has not been dismissed, as the court has to rule on the core constitutional issue concerning equal protection. The District Court has directed the parties to submit a proposed schedule for further proceedings.

In November 2025, former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem announced the termination of Haiti’s TPS designation. The termination was published in the Federal Register (90 Fed. Reg 54733 (Nov. 28, 2025)) and would have ended TPS protections for Haitian beneficiaries. A group of plaintiffs challenged the termination in federal court, arguing that the decision was unlawful and seeking to prevent DHS from implementing it while the litigation proceeded.

In February 2026, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia issued an order staying the effective date of DHS’s termination of Haiti TPS pending judicial review. This injunction preserved TPS protections for affected nationals of Haiti while the court considered the merits of the challenge. The injunction temporarily delayed the termination and allowed Haitian TPS holders to maintain their status and corresponding employment authorization during the litigation.

On June 25, 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court ordered the TPS terminations effective July 27, 2026, and remanded to the lower court to lift the stay. Mullin v. Doe, No. 25-1083. Following receipt of the D.C. Circuit’s mandate on Aug. 4, 2026, the District Court expressly stated that its prior order staying the effective date of DHS’s Haiti TPS termination “is no longer in effect.”

What This Means

Haitian TPS beneficiaries and employers should:

Closely monitor DHS announcements regarding implementation of the termination.

Review the validity of employment authorization as well as any related government guidance.

Evaluate whether Haiti TPS recipients may qualify for another immigration benefit or status.

Consult immigration counsel regarding individualized options and compliance obligations.

While the District Court’s injunction has been lifted, the case remains active, anticipating further litigation. Haitian TPS beneficiaries and employers should continue to monitor developments closely for additional court rulings, DHS guidance, or other administrative actions which may affect the timeline.

Jackson Lewis attorneys will continue to follow this matter and provide updates as new information becomes available.

text:
Texas Democrats in Congress are urging the Trump administration to pause its plan for widespread border security infrastructure inside Big Bend National Park, as a federal contractor working on the project begins to move heavy machinery into the park and local activists warn construction could start at any moment.

On Tuesday, Marfa Public Radio witnessed a bulldozer and multiple trucks bearing the contractor’s name – Southwest Valley Constructors – stationed inside the park near the entrance to Cottonwood Campground, which is situated right next to the U.S.-Mexico border.

The company has been awarded $1.7 billion – one of the largest-ever federal border security contracts – to build a mix of vehicle barriers, surveillance technology and 200 miles of new “patrol roads” across the sprawling West Texas park as part of the Trump administration’s border-wide “Smart Wall” plan. The roads, U.S. Customs and Border Protection has said, could be up to 24 feet wide.

In recent days, local activists have reported seeing the company’s distinct yellow trucks in Big Bend area towns like Terlingua and Alpine.

In an initial statement, a CBP spokesperson told Marfa Public Radio the agency is “in the initial stages of planning and design of this project.” In response to follow-up questions Wednesday, the agency said that “construction crews are onsite re-grading roads that were damaged by recent storms; these roads are required for access to conduct surveys,” though a spokesperson denied that the project itself had officially started.

Last week, most of Texas’ Democratic Congressional delegation penned a letter to Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin and other border agency leaders, outlining their concerns about the plan for the park.

The patrol road route is slated to cross Mariscal Mountain, which rises 1,700 feet above the Rio Grande along the park’s southeastern boundary.

In the letter, the lawmakers raised concerns about the possibility of dirt and rock debris or construction-related materials falling into the river and altering its normal flow. The lawmakers said that kind of impact on the river would violate the 1970 Boundary Treaty – an agreement between the U.S. and Mexico outlining rules for protecting the river.

They also worried about the potential use of explosives for the project.

“The terrain of Mariscal Mountain...would require that the new road be dynamited and bulldozed across Mariscal Mountain along and back from the canyon rim, including its highest cliffs,” the lawmakers wrote, saying such a move would cause “irreparable damage to the Rio Grande” and violate the boundary treaty.

CBP said in a statement the agency “has no plans for blasting of Mariscal Mountain in the Big Bend National Park.”

Notably absent from the list of Democrats who signed the Friday letter was U.S. Rep. Henry Cuellar, a South Texas Democrat. Cuellar echoed CBP’s assurances that it would not use explosives on the mountain in a social media post last week, and in a statement later to Marfa Public Radio Friday said he’d received that information after speaking “directly” with the agency.

“I support strong border security, but it must be carried out responsibly and with respect for Big Bend National Park,” Cuellar said. “I will continue monitoring this project closely and push for DHS transparency throughout the process.”

The National Park Service did not immediately respond to questions about the park project. The agency has refused for months to comment on any development related to the border infrastructure plans and has instead referred all questions on the matter to federal border agencies.

Conservation groups and businesses urge Texas GOP leaders to stop the Big Bend plan

Meanwhile on Tuesday, a coalition of national and local advocacy groups and businesses sent a letter to Texas GOP leaders urging them to block or delay the construction plans in the park.

The letter to Senators John Cornyn and Ted Cruz, along with Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, was signed by national brands like Patagonia and Big Bend area tourism industry businesses. The signers urged the Republican leaders to talk DHS into abandoning plans for physical barriers and roads and to amend federal contracts for the project “to include technology only.”

“Our senators and governor may be the last line of defense standing between access to the Rio Grande and permanent, irreversible damage,” the letter read.

Asked for comment on the letter, Abbott’s press secretary Andrew Mahaleris sent a statement the governor’s office has shared multiple times in recent months, saying Abbott “fully supports using every necessary tool and strategy to aid in the Trump Administration’s deterrence of illegal immigrants attempting to make the dangerous trek across the southern border.”

“Rugged, isolated areas like Big Bend are great opportunities to deploy technology to aid in securing the border,” Mahaleris said.

Former Big Bend superintendent doubts CBP’s promises

Bob Krumenaker, the most recent former superintendent of Big Bend and current chair of the nonprofit Keep Big Bend Wild, said in an interview Monday it would be “physically impossible” to build a road over Mariscal Mountain without using explosives.

“The goal here is obviously to stop the construction of an absolutely senseless road that would all but destroy Mariscal Mountain, which is pretty much the most remote area in Big Bend National Park,” he said.

Krumenaker argues there are “more effective, less destructive, and far less expensive” ways for CPB to meet its goal of reducing illegal traffic.

“There’s no logic,” he said. “ It looks like they’re gonna do all sorts of things, which are almost the most destructive things that they can do for virtually no purpose.”

Krumenaker said he does not expect a response to the letter.

“There is no indication that they are listening,” Krumenaker said. “ It is incredibly disheartening to see the federal government that I worked for for 41 years treat its citizens this way.”

In its statement to Marfa Public Radio, CBP said the agency has been in close communication with the national park service “to ensure that access to the Rio Grande River and hiking trails such as the Mariscal trail remain accessible at the park during and after construction.”

Mary Cantrell contributed reporting from Big Bend National Park.

text:
CHICAGO (AP) — The Trump administration has awarded a $150 million contract to give legal representation to migrant children traveling alone to the U.S. to a small Texas law firm with ties to the administration but little experience in immigration law, prompting legal aid groups who’ve long represented those children to warn that the move could make them vulnerable to deportation.

The contract to the Houston-based Burke Law Group comes as the Trump administration ramps up its mass deportation campaign across the country and after the administration last week let a key contract with a network of legal groups working with immigrant children around the country expire with no replacement. The providers have increasingly raised worries that children won’t have the experienced legal help they need at a time when the administration is intensifying efforts to remove people from the country.

Michael Lukens, who heads the Amica Center, called the idea that the administration had given the sole-source contract to the Texas firm “upsetting and shocking.”

“It really does forebode a situation where children are going to get no meaningful due process, no meaningful day in court. We cannot have a random law firm entrusted to take care of children,” Lukens said.

The groups said the contract announced Tuesday only applies to the children currently held in government-run shelters and that the government would need to issue another contract covering services for migrant children outside the shelter system. Lukens said that there are currently about 1,800 children living in shelters, and roughly 22,000 living outside with sponsors, such as family members.

The Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees the government agency responsible for caring for unaccompanied migrant children, did not respond to requests for comment.

Contract goes to firm with Trump administration ties

The Trump administration announced late Tuesday that they were hiring the Houston-based Burke to provide legal services to unaccompanied children. The year-long contract starts August 15.

Only two of the 25 lawyers listed on the firm’s website on Wednesday morning claim relevant experience in immigration law in their biographies.

Many of the others at the firm are corporate lawyers with ties to conservative causes and to President Trump. The firm’s founder, Marcella Burke, served in Trump’s first administration as a lawyer in the Environmental Protection Agency and the Department of the Interior.

Others on its roster include Justin Shubow, the leading supporter of Trump’s efforts to require federal buildings to adhere to classical and traditional architectural styles, and a former Trump appointee to the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts. Prominent conservative legal scholar Ilya Shapiro is listed as a “senior counsel.”

The firm and the founder didn’t immediately return messages seeking comment.

The notice says Burke’s contract is a “single source cooperative agreement,” which means the administration picked the firm without a competitive bidding process. It did not offer a justification for bypassing standard bidding rules.

Government required to facilitate legal representation

Migrant children alone are viewed as especially vulnerable because of their age and are usually entrusted to U.S. government care. There are various legal protections that apply to them once they’re in the U.S., including the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008, which requires the government to facilitate legal representation for children put into deportation proceedings.

That representation, until recently, was carried out by a network of nearly 100 legal aid providers across the country that provided know-your-rights trainings to children in shelters and directly represented them in court proceedings.

But last Friday marked the last day of that contract and, until late Tuesday, it wasn’t clear if a new contract would be put in place and, if it was, who would do the work.

On top of the contract uncertainty, the legal aid providers say they’ve been struggling to get repaid for work they have already done since last November. The groups say the administration is asking for detailed information about their clients that they say they’re not ethically able to provide.

Legal advocates say they’ve seen other trends that worry them. Since April, the courts started to call dozens of cases at once in so-called “rocket dockets” and immigrant children have had their hearings moved up and given less time to prepare.

Emails to providers, multiple lawyers at courts cause confusion

Other recent occurrences have raised questions about the administration’s intentions regarding the children’s legal representation and caused confusion.

The Associated Press obtained emails sent by the Office of Refugee Resettlement, the federal agency responsible for overseeing unaccompanied migrant children, to lawyers representing migrant children in federal custody. The emails, sent late Tuesday, asked for their clients’ personal identification numbers and requested the lawyers respond within four hours confirming they would be appearing to represent their clients in upcoming hearings.

It was not immediately clear why the administration was making such requests of the children’s lawyers.

Separately, attorneys in courtrooms across the country said their hearings were interrupted by lawyers claiming they had been asked by the Trump administration to take over the children’s cases, without having given prior notice.

At a hearing in Chicago Wednesday morning for unaccompanied detained immigrant children, an attorney who did not represent any of the children suddenly appeared via video stream, in an exchange witnessed by an Associated Press reporter.

The attorney said she was with the U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants, a legal aid group, and that the organization had been contacted by the Office of Refugee Resettlement to “appear on behalf” of children without legal representation due to a “gap in legal services.” She said her organization had received the children’s private information, including their names and identifying numbers, from the federal government.

The judge said that since all the children already had lawyers, he wasn’t going to allow anyone to watch on the video stream, and the outside attorney dropped off.

Laura Smith, an attorney representing some of the children, expressed confusion about why the person was there: “It sounds like this is a person who has my client’s information.”

The U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants referred questions from The Associated Press to HHS’s Office of Refugee Resettlement.

Alexa Sendukas, the managing attorney at the Galveston Houston Immigrant Representation Project, said one of her organization’s attorneys witnessed a similar confusion play out in court Wednesday morning in Houston and that her organization had heard of similar situations in other courtrooms across the country.

__

Santana reported from Sacramento, Gonzalez reported from McAllen, Texas, and Foley reported from Iowa City, Iowa.

text:
Two police officers have been injured after a second night of disorder in a market town which has seen anti-immigration protests.

Norfolk Police said "significant police resources" were deployed to Thetford on Wednesday to maintain public safety, after a large group gathered on Clover Way.

The force said members of the group "became physically aggressive towards officers – a male officer was struck with a rock and a female officer was seriously bitten, breaking the skin."

Assistant chief constable Julie Dean said: "We will not stand by and allow violence to take place, whether that is directed towards members of the public, local residents or police officers carrying out their duties."

The scenes followed unrest on Tuesday in St John's Way, Bracken Road and Elm Road, when properties were damaged with windows smashed and fences broken, and people attempted to break into a residential property, police said.

Witnesses reported a crowd of more than 200 people in Clover Way, with eggs and rocks thrown at houses and chants of "We want them out".

The police then separated the protesters into two groups before moving them away from the area.

The Labour MP for South West Norfolk, Terry Jermy, said the "ugly scenes in Thetford over the past few days have been difficult to watch and are deeply concerning".

A man in his 30s was arrested on suspicion of a public order offence on Wednesday afternoon following Tuesday's disorder. He was released and issued with a conditional caution.

One man aged in his 40s remains in custody, and a 68-year-old man from Thetford has been charged with possession of an offensive weapon, namely a wooden bat.

ACC Dean promised "robust action" to the disorder, adding: "We will always facilitate and support the right to peaceful protest, and we recognise that people may hold strong views and feelings about issues.

"Our role is to keep people safe. We have a duty to protect everyone in our communities, maintain public order and prevent harm. We will not stand by and allow violence to take place, whether that is directed towards members of the public, local residents or police officers carrying out their duties."

Jermy has previously called on the Home Office to end "secrecy and confusion" around plans to house more asylum seekers in former military barracks – including at RAF Barnham near Thetford.

In a statement he condemned the unrest, saying: "People have been pulled from their homes – a place of safety – and forcibly removed, with reports of members of the public breaking into homes, taking property and smashing windows.

"This would have been utterly terrifying for the people in these properties and also very worrying for neighbouring residents.

"I do not know the immigration status of the people placed in these properties or their legal status, but I know they are human beings that must be afforded the same rights that we all expect in this country.

title: How Air Wisconsin turned Milwaukee Mitchell into a hub for ICE planes
description:
So far this year, planes operating under the Air Wisconsin name have conducted more than 1,350 flights around the country for ICE, including dozens out of Milwaukee Mitchell International Airport, where Air Wisconsin has a hangar.
CSI Aviation and Air Wisconsin did not respond to requests for comment.
Many Air Wisconsin flights go to destinations with known ICE facilities A Milwaukee Journal Sentinel analysis of publicly available flight data shows that Air Wisconsin planes fly in and out of Milwaukee several times a month.
Air Wisconsin planes flew to Alexandria, Louisiana more than anywhere else – more than 700 times since January, from both Milwaukee and other cities, the analysis shows.
After that contract ended in spring 2025, Air Wisconsin stopped passenger service and laid off more than 800 workers.
text:
In recent months, Air Wisconsin has become one of the most widely used carriers for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, responsible for nearly half of all domestic ICE flights in June, according to a plane-tracking group called ICE Flight Monitor.

So far this year, planes operating under the Air Wisconsin name have conducted more than 1,350 flights around the country for ICE, including dozens out of Milwaukee Mitchell International Airport, where Air Wisconsin has a hangar.

Established in 1965, Appleton-based Air Wisconsin primarily flew regional commercial flights. In January, the financially troubled airline sold 13 of its planes, and control of the airline itself, to CSI Aviation, a major government contractor that carries out deportation flights for ICE.

Immigrant detainees themselves are not being flown in and out of Milwaukee Mitchell, said airport spokesman Harold Mester.

Instead, Air Wisconsin is using the airport primarily as a base for maintenance and crew, readying the planes before they make their way to other destinations – often cities with known ICE facilities, the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel found.

The Air Wisconsin fleet has taken on a growing role in the Trump administration's immigration enforcement efforts, from making 50 ICE-related flights around the country in January to more than 500 in May alone, according to ICE Flight Monitor.

The group identifies planes associated with ICE using public records and other sources, tracking flights that have recurring patterns of operation and routes to known ICE detention centers and destinations.

CSI Aviation and Air Wisconsin did not respond to requests for comment. Asked about Air Wisconsin's role with ICE, a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said the agency would "not discuss ongoing or future operations" for security purposes.

Much remains unclear about ICE's flight network, and oversight of the private contractors now working for the agency is limited. Nationwide, ICE-related flights were up 78% in May compared to the same time last year, according to ICE Flight Monitor.

By tracking the flights, the group seeks to bring clarity to a murky system, according to Savi Arvey, director of policy for refugee and immigrant rights at Human Rights First, which runs the monitoring project.

ICE's use of private charter planes "has really created an opaqueness over this entire system that is financed by U.S. taxpayers, and created many hurdles in understanding how this money is being spent [and] who is profiting," Arvey said.

Many Air Wisconsin flights go to destinations with known ICE facilities

A Milwaukee Journal Sentinel analysis of publicly available flight data shows that Air Wisconsin planes fly in and out of Milwaukee several times a month. From Milwaukee, the planes frequently make multi-stop trips over the course of a day or more, hopping from state to state.

Several of the most common destinations for Air Wisconsin planes either have an ICE detention center in the vicinity, such as Harlingen and El Paso – both in Texas – or are stopovers where detainees can be picked up, such as in Ypsilanti, Michigan.

Air Wisconsin planes flew to Alexandria, Louisiana more than anywhere else – more than 700 times since January, from both Milwaukee and other cities, the analysis shows.

The city, in rural Louisiana, is home to a short-term "staging" facility for deportees. The Guardian has reported that about 200 detainees pass through the facility each day and face poor living conditions and limited access to attorneys.

William Rankin, a professor of airport management who worked in airport leadership for 29 years, said Milwaukee makes sense logistically as a central location in the U.S. for planes running routes to the east coast and the south.

Air Wisconsin is likely using its hangar at Milwaukee Mitchell primarily to perform the federally-required maintenance and safety checks on its planes, before flying them elsewhere, he speculated.

Air Wisconsin planes have also run routes within Texas repeatedly since January, the Journal Sentinel's analysis shows: over 70 times each from Harlingen to Killeen, Houston to Harlingen, and Killeen to Houston. Air Wisconsin's parent company, CSI Aviation, is headquartered in Killeen, about 70 miles north of Austin.

ICE Flight Monitor also identified several consistent routes in and out of Milwaukee's Mitchell airport specifically – commonly to airports in Ypsilanti, Michigan; State College, Pennsylvania; Bedford, Massachusetts and elsewhere, before turning south. State College also has an ICE detention center nearby.

Immigrant advocates have criticized ICE for frequently sending people to be detained in faraway states and shackling them while onboard.

Immigrants detained far from home often must seek out a new attorney in the area. Only an attorney licensed to practice in the federal district where the person is detained can file a habeas corpus petition to release them from custody.

"These flights that depart rapidly can make it harder to file habeas claims or just generally provide legal support," said Arvey. "People are being put on board without due process at times, in violation of court orders."

ICE's own handbook says detainees on flights should be restrained with handcuffs, waist chains and leg irons.

People detained by ICE in the Milwaukee area are typically not flown out of the area. Instead, they are usually processed at ICE's downtown Milwaukee office, then transported by bus to detention centers elsewhere in the Midwest, such as in Illinois, Indiana and Kentucky.

Air Wisconsin lease doesn't allow it to transport passengers from Milwaukee

In other U.S. cities, images of handcuffed detainees boarding planes at local airports have sparked condemnation and calls for airport authorities to stop or disavow those operations.

The situation in Milwaukee is different because no detainees appear to be on the planes.

That is outlined in the lease agreement between the Milwaukee airport and Air Wisconsin, which states that only maintenance and training operations are allowed on the property. Passenger transport is not permitted.

Any change in Air Wisconsin's operations would need to be approved by the airport director, the lease says.

The company pays $76,867.70 in rent annually to the airport for the 210,000-square-foot property, said Mester, the airport spokesperson. Air Wisconsin has owned the hangar building at the airport since 2001, but rents the land beneath the hangar.

The hangar, along South Howell Avenue, is in a separate area from the main passenger terminal.

Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reporters did not see any detainees boarding or exiting Air Wisconsin planes on a Friday morning in late June when two ICE-related flights took off from the hangar, bound for Richmond, Virginia and Killeen, Texas. Reporters observed pilots and maintenance workers getting on and off the planes.

The lease term goes through 2033.

Until then, as long as Air Wisconsin and CSI Aviation are following federal rules and the terms of their lease, the Milwaukee airport doesn't have standing to stop planes from shuttling in and out for maintenance, said Rankin, the airport management expert, who teaches at the Florida Institute of Technology's College of Aeronautics.

"It would all be under 'general aviation activity,'" he said. "Airports cannot restrict general aviation operations."

Airport officials in other cities have concluded similarly.

At the Yspilanti airport, on the outskirts of Detroit, the airport authority said in February it cannot do anything to stop ICE contractors from running flights.

At the Bedford airport, outside Boston, where an estimated 6,000 ICE detainees passed through in 2025, the airport director said it is “legally obligated to allow all types of aircraft operations."

Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, who is running for governor, did not respond to a request for comment Aug. 5 about whether he would support renewing the lease. Milwaukee County oversees the airport.

CSI Aviation is nation's top ICE contractor

Before its sale in January, Air Wisconsin went through a stretch of financial turbulence.

Its 50-seat Bombardier CRJ-200 jets once carried out regional commercial flights under contract with American Airlines. After that contract ended in spring 2025, Air Wisconsin stopped passenger service and laid off more than 800 workers.

In January, Air Wisconsin's fleet was sold to two buyers for $110 million, filings show. One buyer was a limited liability corporation called Associated Lease and Finance Group. The other was CSI Aviation.

Both of those companies' fleets – as well as planes still listed directly under Air Wisconsin's name – seem to be flying for ICE, public flight data shows. All fly regularly to Alexandria, Louisiana, where the ICE staging facility is located.

As a result of its contracts with ICE, CSI Aviation's revenues have ballooned from nearly $364 million during President Joe Biden's last year in office to $1.23 billion in the first year of Trumps second term, according to the Project on Government Oversight.

That makes CSI Aviation the No. 1 ICE contractor in the country, according to the nonprofit watchdog group.

CSI Aviation's chief executive, Allen Weh, his wife and his daughter contributed $460,000 to Trump's 2024 campaign, the Project on Government Oversight reported.

Air Wisconsin appears to be hiring. Online job postings for the airline posted between May and July advertise openings for mechanics, inspectors and airplane cleaners. A posting for a first officer position – a pilot – lists two locations for the job: Killeen and Milwaukee.

Sophie Carson is a general assignment reporter who reports on religion and faith, immigrants and refugees and more. Contact her at scarson@gannett.com or 920-323-5758.

Eva Wen is an investigative data reporter. Contact her at qwen@gannett.com.

Mary Spicuzza and Lance Schulteis of the Journal Sentinel contributed to this report.

text:
The Trump administration is set to award a multimillion-dollar contract to a small Texas law firm to provide legal representation for thousands of unaccompanied migrant children in government custody during immigration proceedings.

In a notice published in the Federal Register, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) announced its intent to award the $150 million contract to Burke Law Group, a law firm headquartered in Houston, Texas.

The notice states the contract would "provide legal orientation, legal consultation, and attorney-of-record representation services for eligible unaccompanied alien children" during immigration proceedings and hearings before U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services while the children remain in government custody.

The proposed award comes after legal service providers across the country have said that the administration has withheld $65 million in overdue fees from the previous contract, alleging it is an attempt to force them to turn over confidential information about the migrant children they represent.

Burke Law Group has 26 employees across eight offices, according to its website. Their practices include administrative law, white-collar defense, commercial litigation, securities litigation and other areas.

One of the founders, Marcella Burkey, was a former Trump appointee to the Environmental Protection Agency and the Department of the Interior. Jeffrey Hall, a former employee and founding partner, was appointed and confirmed to serve in the EPA late last year.

Burke Law Group did not immediately respond to ABC News' request for comment.

In December 2023, the Acacia Center for Justice, an immigrant advocacy group, became the prime contract holder with HHS for the Unaccompanied Children Program, overseeing subcontracts with more than 100 service providers that provide legal representation to more than 20,000 unaccompanied migrant children.

A spokesperson with HHS previously told ABC News that its sub-agency, the Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR), "offered Acacia the opportunity" to receive a new federal contract "based on requirements that include they provide the data on who they represent and that they bill [HHS] when they submit applications for immigration relief." The HHS spokesperson said Acacia refused.

Legal services providers including Acacia have said that ORR was demanding "client-level data that is confidential and legally privileged."

During the Trump administration, Acacia and many of its subcontracted groups have alleged that unaccompanied children and their sponsors are among those being targeted under the administration's immigration crackdown.

In June, DHS agents visited the offices of several Washington-area nonprofit organizations that provide legal services to unaccompanied migrant children. Last year, ABC News reported that the administration was directing immigration agents to track down unaccompanied migrant children in the United States.

He began by thanking the commission for hosting a forum to examine “human rights atrocities” in the United States.
The IACHR, an autonomous body of the Organization of American States, monitors human rights conditions in the hemisphere and hears complaints from civil society about alleged violations.

text:
On Tuesday afternoon, the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights convened in Washington, DC, to hear complaints about excessive use of force and suppression of freedom of expression during protests against immigration enforcement in American cities. One of those who attended and testified at the public hearing was Antonio Romanucci, a Chicago-based civil rights litigation lawyer representing the family of Renee Good, who was fatally shot by a US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent in Minneapolis in January.

He began by thanking the commission for hosting a forum to examine “human rights atrocities” in the United States. “What we saw with Renee,” Romanucci said, “was a federal agent clearly using deadly force without any legal justification, in an extreme manner, shocking the conscience of our country.” Romanucci, who previously secured a settlement in a wrongful death civil rights case on behalf of George Floyd’s family, said “zero federal investigation” resulted in no accountability in Minneapolis, or elsewhere. “I have not seen these atrocities in my 41 years of practice,” he added.

The IACHR, an autonomous body of the Organization of American States, monitors human rights conditions in the hemisphere and hears complaints from civil society about alleged violations. Romanucci, along with Thomas Becker of the University Network for Human Rights, appealed to the commission, requesting a hearing on the US government’s actions against protesters, journalists, and bystanders at demonstrations opposing the Trump administration’s immigration policies.

“As Donald Trump attacks the courts, weaponizes the Department of Justice, and targets attorneys who challenge his administration,” Romanucci and Becker explained in an opinion piece published in the Guardian previewing the hearing, “we have been forced to seek justice beyond our borders.” They added: “Never before had the commission granted such a hearing, but the extraordinary nature of the Trump administration’s actions…warrants international scrutiny.”

A press release said this marked the first time the IACHR, which doesn’t have enforcement authority, held such a thematic hearing on freedom of expression and the right to peaceful assembly in the United States. “For years, the Commission has heard testimony about the attacks on protesters carried out by some of the region’s most repressive dictatorships,” James Cavallaro, former president of the IACHR, said in a statement. “Now, it is the United States that will be called to answer for these abuses.”

Rev. David Black, a pastor of the First Presbyterian Church of Chicago, was one of the speakers. He recounted how in September 2025, he was wearing his clerical collar when he joined a protest outside the ICE detention facility in Broadview to say a prayer and stand in solidarity with the immigrant detainees. “My words were confrontational,” Rev. Black told the commission. “They were also peaceful.”

He said federal agents fired pepper-balls at him at least seven times, hitting his head, face, torso, arms, and legs. Other protesters tried to cover him, he said, but agents in full armor forced him down and sprayed the pastor with a chemical irritant. Rev. Black, who was part of a federal lawsuit against the US government last year decrying a “pattern of extreme brutality” by federal agents, recalled struggling to breathe. “What happened to me was not an isolated incident,” he said, stating that clergy have been “repeatedly assaulted” outside detention centers and prevented from ministering inside.

The delegation also condemned the Trump administration’s efforts to label protesters as domestic terrorists. Boston University law professor Susan Akram called the policies “blatantly illegal and draconian” and part of a “campaign to criminalize dissent, free expression, and ideologies that this administration dislikes.” Akram said the measures violated international law and “are frankly reviving McCarthyism in the United States.”

Andrea Pochak, one of the IACHR commissioners, said priests, journalists, human rights lawyers, and immigrants are not terrorists. She also inquired about cases in which federal agents engaged in excessive use of force had been disciplined or criminally charged. “The system of accountability is broken,” said Locke Bowman, an attorney representing Rev. Black and two other Chicago residents who have filed claims against the Department of Homeland Security.

The US government provided little in the way of response. Acting Deputy Chief of Mission to the OAS Julianna Aynes-Neville declined to answer questions, citing ongoing litigation. “I am circumscribed in what I am able to say today,” she said. “The United States must once again register dissatisfaction with the decision to convene this hearing on these matters.” She urged the commission to redirect its attention to backlogged cases and countries with “weak or nonexistent protections” for freedom of expression.

Cavallaro, the former president of IACHR, urged the commission to visit the United States to observe the human rights situation in the country. “If there’s nothing to hide, if the system is working, if cases are investigated, if abuses are addressed,” he said, addressing the US representatives, “please show that to the commission.”

“Without any transparent investigation there will never be any discipline,” Romanucci, the lawyer for Renee Good’s family, said, “there will never be any accountability.” After the hearing, Romanucci told Mother Jones the government’s evasiveness at the hearing mirrored its handling of Good’s killing. “Not only do we hear common design in justifying the narrative when there is deadly force or excessive force used,” he said, “this also, to me, is a common design of not answering questions or releasing information in order to make this process more transparent.”

text:
Last week, the White House launched its new Freedom Haulers initiative, a program that aims to remove illegal alien and non-English speaking commercial truck drivers from American roads and highways. As part of the Trump administration’s efforts to combat fraud and illegal immigration, the program would replace these drivers and discourage states from giving them commercial driver’s licenses (CDLs) by opening pathways to hire U.S. military veterans.

The program was rolled out after the Department of Transportation (DOT) and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced that they had forced states to cancel over 28,000 CDLs that were illegally issued and removed over 9,500 unqualified training schools from the registry of accepted providers. DOT also issued a final rule earlier this year to prevent foreign nationals from obtaining licenses for commercial vehicles.

Federal data indicates that in 2025 alone, at least 17 fatal crashes and 30 deaths in were caused by unqualified foreign drivers. An alarming number of cases have piled up this year, too, including the following:

Bekzhan Beishekeev, an illegal immigrant from Kyrgyzstan holding a Pennsylvania CDL, allegedly failed to brake on an Indiana highway and swerved into a van, killing four people.

Haitian national Michael Bon, an illegal alien who was released into the United States under the administration held a Massachusetts CDL and was charged after his rig struck and killed a Pennsylvania State Trooper during a vehicle inspection.

Uzbek national Bekhzod Asrarov, who entered the U.S. in 2024 through the diversity visa lottery, allegedly rear-ended and killed college athlete Tobias Forsythe. He held an Ohio commercial driver’s license (CDL) despite speaking no English.

text:
On June 5, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) published a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM), Clarification of Discretionary Employment Authorization for Certain Aliens, which would limit work authorization for parolees, deferred action recipients, and aliens awaiting deportation on orders of supervision (OSUP). FAIR has submitted a public comment in support of the proposed rule.

Parole is a narrow legal authority that allows DHS to temporarily allow otherwise inadmissible aliens into the country for urgent humanitarian reasons or significant public benefit, such as critical medical care or testifying in a trial. However, the Biden administration systematically abused this authority to admit over two million unvetted illegal aliens from nations including Cuba, Haiti, Nicaragua, Venezuela, and Afghanistan, while also shielding illegal aliens already present in the country from deportation through the legal fiction known as “parole-in-place.” These aliens were indiscriminately given work authorization, incentivizing further illegal immigration.

The DHS rule requires the covered classes of aliens to establish both economic necessity and discretionary merit, replacing the policy of automatically granting work permits with individualized review. Additionally, it restricts work authorization for aliens with a criminal history, requires biometrics with applications, and conditions renewals on employment with an E-Verify-participating employer, all much-needed safeguards for the work permit process.

FAIR’s comment proposes several recommendations for additional reforms. Notably, DHS should end the practice of granting work permits to aliens eligible for parole and provide for existing permits to expire immediately upon an alien receiving a final order of removal. To assess how work authorization for aliens impacts U.S. workers, DHS should coordinate with DOL’s Office of Immigration Policy (OIP) to carry out sectoral labor market analyses.

While this proposed rule reflects a continued trend of positive executive branch action by the Trump administration, FAIR encourages Congress to pass permanent statutory changes, namely H.R. 9773, the Permanent Trump Secure Border Act, which would reduce the ability of the DHS Secretary to grant parole while also reforming asylum and closing several other loopholes that the Biden administration exploited to facilitate illegal immigration.

text:
For 75 years, the 1951 Refugee Convention has served as a global commitment to protect refugees, and as a tool for states to manage global displacement. But today, many of the world’s 41 million refugees face attacks on their rights and governments that seek to return them to harm.

We reflect on the history of the Convention, how this foundational document has served refugees and governments over the years, and the failure of many states to meet their obligations to protect refugees today.

In this episode, we hear from scholar James Hathaway about the objectives, intentions, and limitations of the Convention. He discusses how the Convention balances states’ interests and refugee rights and offers ideas to improve international systems and enhance refugee protection considering current political realities. Then we sit down with Human Rights First’s Eleanor Acer who unpacks how governments, including the Trump administration, are undermining the core tenets of refugee protection and mischaracterizing global displacement dynamics. She offers potential reforms to ensure the Convention is relevant to today’s world.
